utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor against Dusko Tadic, case IT-94-1-T.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. This is a hearing on the Defence motion regarding jurisdiction of the Tribunal. May I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the Tribunal pleases, I appear with my friend Mr. Fenrick and Mr. Tieger and assisted by Professor Maron and Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the Tribunal pleases, in the Defence bench you will see on my far left side, Miss Karin Volgers who is an assistant; next to her you will see Mr. Simic who is counsel in this case; next to me on my left side, Mr. Milan Vujin, who is co-counsel, myself is Michail Wladimiroff, right, far right, you will see Mr. Emile Van Der Does de Willebois, who is an assistant, and between him and myself Mr. Orie who is co-counsel for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, you will be presenting the argument for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will, although Mr. Vujin will make a short statement also -- I announced that to the Registrar -- and Mr. Orie will make a statement too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. For the Prosecutor, who will present their argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will present part of the argument and Mr. Fenrick will present the other part of the argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, the Chamber had indicated that we would issue today our opinion on the motion for protective measures that the Prosecutor has filed; we will not do that today. We received your submissions, Mr. Wladimiroff, on I guess it was 14th July. We also received a reply from the Prosecutor on 21st, I believe, July. So we will endeavour to prepare our opinion and decision with respect to that motion. It is hoped that we will be able to render that decision at the same time that we render the decision regarding the motion that we are hearing this morning. It may be an ambitious endeavour, but we are hoping that we will render that decision on jurisdiction on August 10th. One other preliminary matter (and it has to do with the attachments to the motion on jurisdiction) the Prosecutor has provided us with three volumes, I believe, of attachments and, Mr. Wladimiroff, you also provided the Chamber with some attachments. I do not believe that we have everything that you have cited in your brief. So at the close of this hearing, or at least at the close of today, I would ask you to meet with our senior judicial Officer, our legal Officer, Ms. Featherstone, to go over with her what we are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because we want something more to read!

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I am sorry for that. I will take care.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. We will proceed this morning until about 11.30. At 11.30 we will recess, perhaps, for a half hour. We will then return at 12 o'clock an proceed from 12.00 until 1.00, and then have a lunch recess from 1.00 until 2.30. Then we will come back and continue. We will probably end our proceeding today at 5 o'clock, but if it looks like we are close to hearing arguments of the parties, we will proceed a little later. Very good. Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff, would you like to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I will. What I will do is make a very short introduction, then I will discuss the right of your Trial Chamber to review the decision of the Security Council. Then, of course, I will address the decision itself, then Mr. Orie will go into the matter of primacy. After him Mr. Vujin address the court with a short statement. Finally, I will discuss the subject matter of jurisdiction. Then before going into the substance of the matter, I would like to make a few observations concerning the character of the case, since the argumentation of the prosecution in its response to our motion seems to be founded upon principles of international law without taking into account principles of criminal law. It can do no harm to emphasise that the Tadic case is a criminal trial being heard by an exclusive criminal court and not a dispute between states coming before a court under international law. Unlike international law, where the concepts and the customs are often defined quite vaguely and that, clearly, are approached more from a policy and, therefore, a political perspective than from a legal point of view, the criminal debate is sharply demarcated by demands o legality and legitimacy. The Defence missed this aspect in the Prosecution's approach. Furthermore, one should realise that a Tribunal cannot be compared to the International Court of Justice. We found a lot of references in the response of the Prosecution to rulings of the International Court, but we feel that since the Tribunal, unlike the International Court of Justice that can only give advisory opinions and decisions that do not directly affect an individual and that are not enforceable against individuals, the Tribunal can impose a punishments that may be executed against the will of those concerned. In the criminal case against Tadic, what is relevant is not so much the question of what is desirable in the exclusive context of international law from a global-political point of view, but the issues of what is legitimate in a criminal legal context. Then our motion raises three questions: Has the Tribunal been established by law? Does the Tribunal have primacy over competent domestic courts and, last, but not least, does the Tribunal have jurisdiction in the case of Dusko Tadic? The first question concerning the establishment of the Tribunal raises a number of separate questions. I shall start my commentary on the motion with the question of whether the Tribunal, being an independent Tribunal, is competent to the judge whether itself has been established by law. The position of the Defence with respect to the competence of the Tribunal to examine and to judge the legitimacy of the establishment of the Tribunal by the Security Council is, as was argued by the Prosecution, beyond its competence. James C. O'Brien, for example, raised this issue in 1993 in the American Journal of International Law, I quote: "Perhaps more importantly, the Yugoslav Tribunal is accountable to the defendants, who are not prohibited from challenging its authority, as they were under the Nuremberg Charter. The Tribunal may -- and probably should -- decide that it lacks the power to consider the legitimacy of the Security Council's actions to establish it, because it would require that it construe the powers of the Security Council. If it will reach this decision, if it does, only after deciding whether the defendants' arguments succeed or fail on their merits. The Tribunal will gain legitimacy with each exchange of this issue". (James O'Brien "Current Developments", American Journal of International Law, 1993, volume 87, page 643). Then, from his editorial in the American Journal of International Law of 1994, it seems to me that Theodor Maron is advocating that the Tribunal is not bound by the opinion of the Security Council on the international character of conflicts, and I suggest that this authoritative author is not convinced that the Tribunal has no power whatsoever to consider the legitimacy of the Security Council's actions to establish it either. I quote: "In contrast to the Nuremberg Charter, the Statute of the ad hoc tribunal does not preclude challenges of its authority by defendants. The tribunal may rule on challenges concerning the international character of the conflicts and, indeed, other jurisdictional matters. Whether it will be ready assertively to question the Security Council's resolution under which it was established, or its constitutive charter, the Statute, is another matter." The Defence has, as suggested by O'Brien, which seems to be on the side of Prosecution in this matter, raised (in its motion and brief) arguments opposing the legitimacy of the establishment by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, may I ask you a question, because I also read that paper by Mr. O'Brien and I am not sure that I understood what he was saying. The way that I read it, he seemed to have said, well, the Tribunal would not have power to pass on the decision of the Security Council. However, it would help international lawyers if we said something about it. Is that the way you read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does that mean exactly? Should we just write for ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It seems to that he is not taking a ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- educational purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: -- definite position. He raised a question. He is not making any definite statement about it in the sense of you cannot; he doubt whether it will be possible, but what he is arguing is it should be discussed. That is how I read it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will be discussing it, that is for sure!

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is what I am going to d because today we will elaborate all arguments and we are confident that on the merits of these arguments your Trial Chamber will find that the establishment of the Tribunal was ill-founded. The Tribunal's competence to judge this question that was raised by the Prosecution derives, in the Defence's opinion, from the general principle of justice, that one of the preconditions that derives from the principle of justice that we have to comply with human rights is that a criminal court will be legitimately established. It is communis opinio that general principles of law, as is recognised in Article 38 of the Statute of International Court of Justice, belong to well-established, customary international law. The same applies to basic principles of human rights as recognised in international covenants. One of the principles is that everyone who has been charged with a criminal offence is entitled to a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial Tribunal established by law. This basic human right is recognised in the most important international instruments on this matter, like Article 14(1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as well as Article 6(1) of the European Convention on Human Rights. In this connection I may quote again James O'Brien's article "Current Developments": "Defendants are entitled to the rights provided in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights". Then, in the light of these guarantees to a fair trial, it is a completely legitimate defence to question the origin of the jurisdiction. If the establishment of a court were to be judged exclusively by the founder, in this case the Security Council, the guarantee to legality would be devoid of all meaning. Should the judge be bound by the founders' judgement (and purpose) concerning the legality of the establishment, the guarantee of independence would be limited to a considerable degree. So, I emphasise two elements of the aforementioned principles of international human rights law that are relevant today: independence of the court and establishment of the court by law. To start with the last element, the establishment of the court by law. The requirement that a court should be established by law expresses the importance of the legality in the system in criminal law and procedure. In accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, punishability and competence to punish can only derive from law. The establishment of a criminal court is, therefore, an important issue that cannot simply be taken for granted. In the light of the guarantees granted to the accused founded in human rights, the accused cannot be denied the right to challenge the establishment of the court in his case. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this case explicitly provide for the possibility of the accused to challenge the Tribunal's jurisdiction. The Defence mentioned in rule 73(A)(i) is in no way limited as far as the various aspects of the jurisdiction (its origin, scope and functioning) are concerned. This makes good sense since the Tribunal is not a permanent court so that the question of its own jurisdiction as an ad hoc tribunal is likely to raise questions concerning the legality. Moreover, the compulsory jurisdiction of the Tribunal as far as its administration of justice in criminal cases is concerned (unlike the ICJ's jurisdiction, which is founded upon the explicit acceptance thereof by the parties in the case, who could be said to make use of the existence of the permanent presence of that court) implies for the Tribunal the possibility of having the legality of the jurisdiction fully examined. Since there is no voluntary arrangement concerning the acceptance of jurisdiction, as in the ICJ system, there is every reason to consider the Tribunal, attributed with compulsory jurisdiction and, moreover, a primacy over other courts, fully competent to examine its own jurisdiction. As far as the other element is concerned, independence, independence implies that -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff. Let me ask you one other question, if I may, before you leave the Rules: You refer to Rule 73. Of course, that is a rule that was adopted by the judges -- we drafted those Rules -- but where in the Statute is there an indication that this Tribunal has power to review the decision of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As we see it, your Honour, the matter has not been provided with in the Statute. The Statute just leaves it open. So it seems to the Defence that where there is no regulation on this matter in the Statute, the judges by drafting rule 73(A)(i) fills that gap, and provided any possibility to challenge the jurisdiction which was not provided for in the Statute. So there are no limits in the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does Article 1 mean to you then, the competence of the International Tribunal -- Article 1 of the Statute? It describes the power that the Tribunal has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely, but it does not implicate that by the wording of Article 1 of the Statute that you are not allowed to examine and judge the establishment of the court. At least we do not read in Article 1 such limitation, because systematically spoken, one might argue that if you would read Article 1 in a very limited way, one might wonder whether the court has competence, for example, to punish witnesses who do not speak the truth, because that would be out of the framework of Article 1, will it not? So for that reason we feel that Article 1 is not a limitation for your competence, as we discussed today, and you have filled in that gap by Article 74(A)(i) and, indeed, you did, as we see it, with respect to witnesses and other matters which may seem beyond the scope of Article 1. So, a reasonable explanation of Article 1 is that it does not give you a limitation to judge the matter we discuss today. I will proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That means really that you are drawing an analogy between the power to punish for perjury which may or may not be inherent in a court and the ability of the court to challenge jurisdiction, its own jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, because if you opened the possibility, as is the case in 74, it is inherent to that possibility that you have a full examination, where 74 does not limit the scope of this examination; it just simply says that you can challenge the jurisdiction. That is it -- period. So there is nothing in the rule that says that you are limited to, for example, jurisdiction on Article 2 up to 5 or any other Article. It just says "jurisdiction" as such. So, inherent to this provision, in our view, you should examine all parts of it. For that reason, we argue you have a right to review.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you talk about the powers that the Security Council has ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- with respect to enforcement measure?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will address that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because perhaps that may relate in a sense to the power of this Tribunal to challenge resolutions of the Security Council, particularly the way the ICJ has treated that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will come to that point and I will address that issue, but I separate question whether the Security Council was able to do what it did from, to start with, is your court competent to review? As I see it from the provisions of human rights, it follows that a defendant, an accused, has the right to challenge the establishment by law and that implicates that you have to review the matter by law and, coming to that point, I have argued what I did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any particular reference with respect to the provisions of human rights, or are you saying that that is inherent in the right to have a fair trial, that before you can have a fair trial you should be entitled to challenge the jurisdictional base?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Defence has no doubt that the right to a fair trial, which is also provided for in the Statute, also implicates a provision that is establishment of the court by law. You will find it in the International Covenant, Article 4, and European Covenant, Article 6. As I already told your court, the reference I made was James O'Brien who stipulates that, indeed, the accused has this right to a fair trial in this sense. So we feel that we could argue that your court will have to examine the establishment by law as an inherent provision of human rights.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: To a fair trial, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: To a fair trial, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that Professor Maron has taken the position that there is a right of the Tribunal to challenge the decision of the Security Council? You sort of left that open.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Neither is Professor Maron very definite on this point. It seems to us that he leaves the question also open. We have used that argument to demonstrate that it is not a res judicata. It is not a matter not to be discussed, as was the argument of the Prosecution. We feel the matter is still open. It is not decided yet. So we should discuss the matter as we have done. Then, as far as the other element is concerned, independence implies that the judge should be able to form his judgement on the basis of his own free opinion concerning the facts and the legal grounds without being in any way bound by the parties in the case or the organ that appointed him or her. As an independent judgement concerning the facts and legal grounds implies that the judge should have full freedom to take into account all those aspects which he deems relevant in a particular case, and that in forming an opinion he is not to be bound by the opinions or facts and legal matters voiced by other non-legal bodies. It is clear that the question of the jurisdiction could be such a relevant aspect of this kind. In this case that means that your Trial Chamber on the basis of Rule 73(A)(i) is free to examine this question in its full extent; both as far as factual and as far as legal aspects are concerned without being bound by the opinions that have been voiced by the Security Council or any other organ of the United Nations. The arguments put forward by the Prosecutor contesting the Tribunal's competence to examine the establishment independently failed to take into account the fundamental requirements of a fair criminal trial. As far as the international legal argument is concerned, the Defence does not find the response convincing. I will come to that later. To start with, the Defence considers it unthinkable that your Trial Chamber should consider its itself fully bound by the opinion of the UN Security Council on one or more aspects of the jurisdiction, such as the competence to establish the Tribunal and (it is, therefore, unthinkable that the Tribunal) should not examine the plea raised by the Defence on this issue. Such a position would amount to a denial of Mr. Tadic's right (as has been recognised in international law) to be tried by an independent judge. Moreover, it would amount to neglecting your duty to examine a plea based on a human right (which is also recognised in international law) and that is human right to be tried by a court established by law. In this respect, I would like to point out the Expenses case as put forward by the Prosecution in which the International Court of Justice says, among others: "Each organ must, in the first place at least, determine its own jurisdiction." We feel that this does not mean that the exercise of jurisdiction beyond powers granted in the Charter cannot be challenged. Contrary to that which is argued in the response, the case law of the International Court of Justice does not prevent the court from a limited judicial review of the decisions of the UN organs. From the Namibia Advisory Opinion, it is clear that, although the legitimacy or the conformity to the Charter of a General Assembly resolution is not the subject of the opinion requested, the International Court of Justice in exercising its judicial function does pay attention to the objections raised, before deciding what the consequences of certain resolutions would be. From consideration 115 it is clear that those decisions, "were adopted in conformity with the purposes and principles of the Charter and in accordance with its Articles 24 and 25". In other words, apparently the Court has judged whether the basis of the resolution is well founded, otherwise we cannot understand why this has been ruled in this wording. From the Lockerbie case it is clear that this is about a decision at the time when the case was before the Court to hear the merits of the request for provisional measures. It is provisionally determined that prima facie the Security Council's decision appears to be valid. For a further discussion on this question, I refer to what is said later on in that case. This consideration implies -- the consideration that prima facie the Security Council's decision appears to be valid -- that the legitimacy of the decision taken by an UN-organ can be subject to a judgement. In this respect -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you with respect to Lockerbie and the Expenses case. In Lockerbie did the ICJ pass on the legitimacy of that resolution, or did they instead find that Article 103 required that the states defer to that resolution, even though there were conventions that might require them to take different action? Did the ICJ actually review and make a decision as to the validity of resolution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As we read it, there was not an explicit decision on the matter. The issue itself played a role and, as we read it, such a role, that if it did not comply, then the ruling would have addressed that matter. So it means implicitly that the ICJ looked into the matter and found that, on the face of it, the decision appears to be valid and for that reason there was no reason to make any decision on that matter. So, implicitly, they have viewed the matter but did not review it because there was no reason to. So, in our opinion, it means that they did not ignore it by reasons we are not in the position to go into the matter. They did, as a matter of fact, otherwise it is not to understand why they said that, on the face of it, the decision appears to be valid. It would be a useless thing to say if you had not given it a thought. So we feel that the decision in this case implicates that the legitimacy is a part of the considerations of the court and that it should also be your consideration too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the Expenses case, did that administrative Tribunal of the UN, did that Tribunal or Commission, decide its own jurisdiction? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have not referred to the Expenses case in that respect. The reference I made to the Expenses case is to demonstrate that that case does not mean that the exercise of jurisdiction may not be challenged, because in the case the judge says that each organ must in the first place determine its own jurisdiction -- each organ, sorry. That means that if an organ may do so, you are an organ of the United Nations, you may determine your own jurisdiction too. That is the way we use the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even though there they were referring, I gather, to the General Assembly or no -- I do not -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but there is no reason to believe that the position of the organ General Assembly 3 would differ from this organ being a Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am not quite clear in the way in which you are using the expression "jurisdiction". Clearly enough 73, rule 73(A), confers power to challenge jurisdiction. If one looks at Article 1 of our Statute, there are at least three areas of jurisdiction that the Tribunal would have to have regard to, serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory and since 1991. So that if a charge was brought and it occurred, for instance, it related to matters before 1991, clearly, there would be no jurisdiction. That would be a matter that the Tribunal would, clearly, have to look at. What you are really dealing with is not jurisdiction; it is the validity of the establishment of the Tribunal, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is to be disputed, I am afraid. If the establishment of the Tribunal is not according to the powers granted to the Security Council, to say it shortly, was not accordance with the Charter, and if the argument is valid, that the establishment was not by law for that reason, we believe that, not on the basis of the Statute itself, but as an inherent part of having jurisdiction to try people, the Tribunal should examine as an aspect of its jurisdiction whether this jurisdiction raised from a valid establishment, because if the jurisdiction is not established on a valid basis, then you will not be able to come to the real issue and that is, as you said: Do we have jurisdiction in Article 1, 2 and so on? So it is an aspect you cannot ignore. Jurisdiction implicates that if the basis of the jurisdiction is not there, there is no jurisdiction. So you have to examine, and that is what we are asking you to examine, the basis of your own jurisdiction and not the results of the jurisdiction, that is, does the jurisdiction have any meaning in connection with the person or connection with the territory or in connection with subject matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, so it is not at all the breadth of our jurisdiction that you are challenging; it is the very existence of the Tribunal and whether it was validly established?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree on that, but it may be a playing of words, but we feel it as an aspect of jurisdiction and not as a separate matter which has nothing to do with jurisdiction and should be discussed on another basis. We feel it is an aspect of the jurisdiction matter itself. Let me just see where I landed. I made some remarks about the Lockerbie case and in this connection I may refer to the annotation of Christian Tomuschat of the Lockerbie case in The Review of 1992 (No. 48, page 48). I quote: "The Security Council is not sacrosanct and if the World Court is called upon to apply a resolution of the Security Council it must be satisfied that the resolution concerned complies with the requirements of lawfulness as established by the UN Charter." The opinion put forward implicitly in the Prosecution's argument, namely, that the Security Council is completely competent to determine its own competence -- the Germans call this, as you know, the Kompetenz-Kompetenz -- would render the UN Charter completely meaningless as a source of legal protection. From the Lockerbie case, which I just mentioned, it is clear that, in judging the consequences of the Security Council's resolutions, the question of whether the Security Council has not exceeded its powers in adopting those resolutions is, indeed, taken into account. Clearly, also in international law the question of legality is an important issue. Then, contrary to the Prosecution's point of view, this conclusion is not precluded, as the Prosecution seems to believe, by the Expenses Advisory Opinion. This case concerns a different matter altogether. This case turns on the issue of whether members of the United Nations were bound by the decisions of the organisation's organs (whether they were competent to make them or not). In that context the organisation is indeed bound by such decisions. That is a different position from the case we have here at hand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, before you leave that issue, when you speak of "jurisdiction" are you including not only the power of the Tribunal but also the appropriateness of the Tribunal passing on what the Prosecutor would consider to be political questions and we might consider to be non-justiciable political questions, particularly the finding by the Security Council that there was a threat to peace because of the activities in the former Yugoslavia? Is there any criteria for us, as judges, to use in reviewing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think I will come to that later ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. That is fine. You can talk about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: -- in the statement I have prepared. From this case law it will be clear that the position of the Court is probably such that it is not competent to subject the decisions of UN-organs to a constitutional review automatically, as constitutional courts in certain member-states (such as Germany) can do. But if the question is raised explicitly, then the Court, as we see it, can answer legal questions regarding the powers of UN-organs, apparently with a view to the independent judgement of their legality. For reasons mentioned earlier, this cannot be less so in criminal law. In the Namibia Advisory Opinion, after the Court had judged the basis of the resolution, the precise contents of the measures and their suitability was left to the political organ. I believe that in a case which is not of a purely international legal nature, as in this criminal case, what is at stake are not "usual measures", but a special institution charged with the administration of criminal justice to individuals. That is quite a different position. In that case the exact determination of the contents of the measures cannot be left exclusively to political organs. In the case of the Tribunal, the question centres on the foundation of the measure that established it. Therefore, the legal review comes down to the question of whether the function exercised by the Tribunal fits into the United Nations constitutional structure. In that respect, we feel that the comparison drawn by the Prosecution with the Tokyo Charter is incorrect. There was no framework against which the Charter, being the result of the exercise of their powers by the Allied Powers and the Supreme Commander, could be tested. The Allied Powers, in this respect not bound by any arrangement concerning the attribution of powers, created their own competence. The Tokyo Charter is, therefore, the result of an original competence, as was the case with the Nuremberg Charter. As far as the Yugoslav Tribunal is concerned, there is a framework against which the Statute, being the result of the Security Council exercising its powers, can be tested, namely, the UN Charter. In this respect the Security Council (unlike the Allied Powers) is bound by its own Charter, created its own competence, and we must now ask ourselves whether it has exceeded its powers as laid down in the UN Charter. In the opinion of the Defence, those powers have been exceeded. I will come to that in a moment. In sum, the Defence, therefore, suggest that a review is not absolutely forbidden and we, therefore, request your Trial Chamber to do so regarding all aspects of the jurisdiction. From this point I will now discuss the matter of the establishment of the Tribunal itself, that is, the powers of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff. With respect to the Charter, the UN Charter, I think it is Article 92, does that not create the International Court of Justice as the principal judicial organ?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think will come to that now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am making a note of all of these things you tell me you are coming back to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I am afraid I will be trapped at the end of this afternoon, but anyhow I will try to address any question you put but, on the other hand, I have tried to follow the pattern of the argument I am trying to develop. The implication of the first aspect of the defence is that the Tribunal cannot found its own jurisdiction upon a decision to establish it which was taken unlawfully. The view behind it is, of course, since the Security Council's decision had no basis in law, the Charter was breached. The argument that the decision by the Security Council to establish the Tribunal under Chapter VII of the Charter was unlawful is, as is clear from the motion, founded upon several sub-arguments. Of these sub-arguments I will only go into the key questions, namely, the objection that according to the Defence the Security Council was not empowered by Chapter VII to establish the Tribunal, secondly, that the establishment is not justified by the existence of threats to peace and security or by certain special circumstances and, finally, that the Security Council cannot take measures that create criminal liability for individuals. In the opinion of the Defence, considerations offered by the first committee (entrusted with drafting the Preambule, Purposes and Principals of the UN Charter) demonstrate that the spirit of the UN Charter starts from the assumption that judicial organs are established either by the General Assembly or in the Charter. It is significant and remarkable in this respect that since the United Nations was founded, no-one, not even the International Law Commission, has ever contemplated the possibility of the Security Council establishing a judicial body under Chapter VII. Before 1993 we believe the idea would have been dismissed as absurd. In the ILC's report of 1993 the argument is considered as to whether a permanent international criminal court should not be created by the General Assembly or the Security Council since these are political organs. This line of reasoning -- the Security Council being a political organ -- holds a fortiori good for the current ad hoc Tribunal. I refer to pages 2804 and 2805. This argument seems logical to me, since decisions of the Security Council, regarding the international legal relationship between states, are usually of a predominantly political nature and normally are based exclusively upon international law. The question of whether the measure adopted by the Security Council is appropriate depends upon the context in which the question is posed. From a purely international legal point of view, the answer could be different than from a criminal point of view. If the issue is the maintenance of peace by way of non-legal instruments, the measures should, undoubtedly, be in accordance with international law. But in the case of specifically legal measures, establishing judicial bodies dealing with criminal law, such decisions by the Security council have to comply to stricter requirements of a different legal nature as well. They should not only be in accordance with international law, but also with general principles of criminal justice and human rights as well as complying with the requirements of ad hoc administration of justice, such as, for example, the requirement of consistency. Where it is probably inherent in politics that the Security Council is not bound to operate in a consistent manner when adopting usual measures, the failure to operate consistently when adopting legal measures with criminal legal consequences with for individuals, may lead to a breach of the principle of a proper administration of justice. The government of the United States in its amicus curiae letter does not demand consistency from the Security Council. This, indeed, is, of course, rather strange taking into account the USA's right of veto regarding, for example, the history of the Vietnam war. Methods and powers of decision-making within the Security Council can result in ad hoc tribunals never being established in conflicts in which one of the five permanent members of the Security Council is involved. This type of (non-permanent) administration of justice ad hoc is founded upon a certain political arbitrariness. Although this right of veto may be acceptable as far as political decisions are concerned, it can certainly not serve as a basis for the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just ask you what you mean by "consistency"? Are you saying that the Security Council can only validly establish a tribunal ad hoc, such as this Tribunal, if it does so in relation to every incident which might conceivably justify such an establishment? Is what you mean by "consistency"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think so. What I am trying to argue is that such a decision may result from a consistent policy that addresses the same problems in a consistent way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So if there had been an establishment of very many ad hoc tribunals, then you would see consistency as satisfied and that would indicate validity of establishment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is very hypothetical but, nevertheless, to start with, it would look much, much better indeed, though I think it is not very realistic to compare it in that way. What I am trying to say is, if the Security Council, for good or bad -- I am not going to judge that -- political reasons, did not address comparable problems in Cambodia, Vietnam and South Africa -- all the countries I have mentioned in the motion -- it is very difficult to understand the consistency of the decision to address the Yugoslav problem in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That, you say, goes to the validity of the establishment of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. It also has implications for the validity of the establishment itself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just follow up on that? That is the kind of question that I was referring to previously, the kind of political question, it seems to me, that makes it inappropriate for a judicial tribunal to review. If we admit that it is a political decision, then what is the scope of our review? We are not politicians. I suppose the question is whether it was legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What we are asking you, your Honour, is not to assess that this is a political decision. What we ask you to do is to see whether this decision, being it political or not, is consistent and could reason, for example, the establishment of this court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When you speak of "consistency" then, should we look at the various conflicts that have existed throughout the world -- I could think of more than you have suggested -- and then make a determination as to whether the failure to establish an ad hoc tribunal for Angola, Mozambique, Haiti, Somalia, Vietnam, whether somehow that then impacts the legality of the Security Council's decision in this instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me put it just very bluntly. What if the Security Council establishes a court that has only jurisdiction to punish people with white hair? Everyone with white hair would challenge the validity of that decision, because that is not consistent with the proper administration of criminal law. Being the Security Council, a political organ or not, they should not have done this. This is far beyond what is reasonable explanation of the powers under the Charter and not consistent with anything they did before.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that, perhaps, rather than comparing the conflict in Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia, with conflicts that have existed throughout the world, instead, perhaps, we should look at what the Security Council determined and make a determination as to whether that was rational and non-arbitrary based upon the evidence that they had ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- rather than comparing it to other conflicts, look at this conflict and determine whether or not it was arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The structure of decision-making within the Security Council prevents, as we see it, it from taking decisions, establishing independent, non-discriminating administration of justice. Let us not forget that it was precisely the United States which withdrew its acceptance of the ICJ's Compulsory Jurisdiction as a consequence of the Nicaragua case. So we should not ignore -- there is always some politic in it -- we should not deal with political questions, but we cannot ignore the political aspect of the matter. Whatever the ins and outs may be, the Defence conclude from this that it has never been the intention to attribute the Security Council with powers enabling it to establish judicial organs. Apart from the Yugoslav and Rwanda Tribunal, there is only one precedent of a judicial organ being established by the Security Council (the Iraqi/Kuwait Compensation Commission and the fund belonging to it). This is about a civil liability, so not a criminal liability, on which the Security Council had already basically decided before establishing this Commission. The reasoning now behind the establishment of your court, the reasoning behind resolution 827, is that the atrocities in the former Yugoslavia themselves constitute threats to international peace and security, and that alternative remedies were exhausted. Using these arguments to focus on the conflict in Yugoslavia is arbitrary since other conflicts would certainly qualify for these characteristics, but no comparable measures were taken by the Security Council. This difference in approach has fuelled speculation that the Security Council has, perhaps, also been partisan to the case of the Serbs' opponents. In the Defence's opinion the establishment of the Tribunal viewed against this background is driven rather by the urge to make a gesture towards the warring parties in former Yugoslavia than by considerations of justice. The argument that a treaty would have frustrated immediate and effective trial seems insignificant if one considers that the United Nations has not established a permanent international criminal court since the 1950s. The constituting organs have to provide, have they not, for timely, adequate administration of justice and it is unacceptable that on grounds of previously being unable to do so the organisation may invoke a kind of emergency situation, thereby ignoring the only legitimate and correct way of establishing an international criminal court. The establishment of the Tribunal is not in the meantime a fait accompli. Such a conclusion can in the Defence opinion not be justified by the Free Zone case. This case has a completely different background from the issue discussed here today, so we do not share the opinion of the Prosecution that this case is relevant for this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Free Zone case. It was raised by the Prosecution. Anyhow, in his statement in the Lockerbie case, President Oda says that a resolution "may have binding force", and note that President Oda did not say "has binding force." I cannot conclude from that, that the Security Council can under all circumstances bind member-states. I recall the observation of Tomuschat that the Court must be satisfied that the resolution concerned complies with the requirements of lawfulness under the UN Charter. Moreover, the background here should not be overlooked. This case is not about the creation of a judicial organ, the Lockerbie case, but about a resolution which should bind member-states. From this angle, it is definitely unimportant whether such a resolution, provided it was adopted in accordance with the positive law of the United Nations, is "in accordance with international law derived from other sources". If, as in this case, the establishment of a judicial organ is at stake, then it follows from the nature of such an organ and the powers attributed to it, which in themselves should be in accordance with international law, that such a resolution should, of course, be in accordance with international law derived from other sources. If that is not the case, the Security Council could establish courts vested with exceptional powers which in civilised states would be considered unacceptable, like prosecuting people only with white hair, for example. At this point I would like to draw a sub-conclusion. From what I have said earlier on, it follows that I submit that the competence of the Security Council to establish the Tribunal cannot be concluded from the travaux preparatoires, whereas, as we said earlier, it is in the nature of the Tribunal that the Security Council is not the organ that should establish a judicial organ. In our motion, I have suggested that Chapter VII of the Charter does not expresis verbis enable the Security Council to establish a criminal Tribunal. Before going into the Security Council's opinion of its own competence, I would like to briefly say that it is remarkable that external arguments justifying such a step, have only arisen after its establishment. I already mentioned that. Before that date, no-one ever claimed that the Security Council could be allowed to establish a Criminal Tribunal. It is so unthinkable that it has never been considered by anyone in literature, neither any academic nor the International Law Commission mentioned it anywhere. It is a non-issue. Only after the establishment of the Yugoslavia Tribunal did the International Law Commission react. The reaction implies no more than an acceptance of the reality of the role of the Security Council has now assumed where humanitarian law is concerned, but the ILC does not say that the Security Council was competent to establish the Tribunal. Coming to this point, the comparison (drawn by the Prosecutor) to Article 23 of the Draft Statute for an International Criminal Court (the ILC report) is, therefore, incorrect. The Security Council's competence under Chapter VII is limited in this report to bringing cases before the Court and does not imply that the Security Council could also establish a Tribunal itself. We certainly not read this in the report ------

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question about the ILC: Does not the Draft Statute for the ILC allow for submissions by the Security Council, even if member-states would not agree with the issue being submitted, and is that not a recognition even on the part of the International Law Commission that there is a role for the Security Council in actually referring cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is what I am going to discuss now, because I do recognise that right, but that right does not imply that the Security Council could also establish a Tribunal by itself. It is a different nature matter, you see. It also follows, if you compare the competence of a State under Article 21 of the Draft, because this right of, should I better say, the competence of a state to defer cases to a court does in turn not imply that the state is competent to establish a court. So I cannot see why Article 23 of the Draft would imply that the Security Council would have that right. It is no argument in favour of the competence to establish a court. It just says nothing more than that, that the Security Council plays a role in this area, and they are entitled to bring cases to this court and just that -- period -- and not any right to establish a Tribunal itself. If I return to the Charter, I emphasise that, although the Security Council does not fulfil a subordinate function, the execution of its powers is certainly limited (if we look into Article 24 at paragraph 2 of the Charter) to those listed under Chapters VI, VII, VIII and XII. I may again suggest that in as far as powers under Chapter VII do not go far enough, it is only the General Assembly which can (under Articles 108 and 109 of the Charter) by way of an amendment of the Charter, substantially alter the balance. Although the General Assembly's powers are generally indeed different from those of the Security Council (see Article 10 and following of the Charter), the Prosecutor's argument that the General Assembly cannot legitimately establish the Tribunal cannot be correct, taking into account Articles 108 and 109 of the Charter. I would just like to point out that the involvement of the General Assembly in the working out of some of the aspects of Tribunal (that is, the appointment of the judges, the questions related to the budget and so on) is a different matter altogether, which only arises after the Tribunal has been established by a legitimate decision. It does not say anything about establish itself. Since the Tribunal is a subsidiary organ, it is impossible to withdraw matters related to the budget, for instance, from the competence of the General Assembly. So, in that context, indeed, the General Assembly has something to do with the Tribunal, but that is not the issue we are addressing today. Let me return to the Security Council again.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just before you do, let us go back to the General Assembly: Are you saying that only the General Assembly has the power to establish a judicial organ or are you saying that it is preferable, that it would have been preferable?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If a Charter does not provide in the establishment of a judicial court, it is the General Assembly's power to amend the Charter and to establish such a court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 29 which gives the Security Council the authority to establish the subsidiary organs, that does not help you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It does help in other cases but not -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It may not help you, what I mean, it does not affect your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you mean. It does not help me in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So, in effect, you are saying there is no power in either of the Security Council or the General Assembly as the Charter now stands, and the Charter would require amendment if there were to be a validly established Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It may be argued that the General Assembly could establish, but I have not elaborated that because that is not the issue we are going to deal with today, but the Royal Road would be by amending the Charter, that is substitute for a treaty, is it not? Let me return to the Security Council again. Although under Article 24 of the Charter, primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security lies with the Security Council, this does not imply that it is within the powers of the Security Council under Chapter VII to establish a judicial organ such as this Tribunal, because the Security Council's powers do not provide it with a blank cheque to take measures which would violate fundamental principles and rules of international law, even if these are not specifically referred to in chapter I or in other provisions of the Charter. The International Court of Justice illustrates this in its Namibia Advisory Opinion, even while pointing out the existence of Security Council's general powers under Article 24 of the Charter, by stating that the Council is no more allowed to do anything which is not specifically prohibited on the basis of its general powers, than it is on the basis of specific authority granted to it elsewhere in the Charter, particularly if this were to violate fundamental human rights. The Prosecutor's argument on the powers under Chapter VII, in fact, come down to claiming that the Security Council can do anything which is not explicitly prohibited from doing and that the General Assembly has nothing to do with that. We cannot accept that. To me, the point of the Charter seems to be that as a structure of coherent rules, it attributes powers to organs and defines powers between organs, but it also binds the exercise of those powers by the organs, meaning no organ can simply do anything it wants to. In short, the freedom assumed by the Security Council to do as it pleases can never go so far as to allow it to determine the framework of Chapter VII itself in the sense that the Security Council determines itself what falls within (or outside of) that framework. A view to the contrary would lead to absurd results. One could, for instance, wonder whether the Security Council would be competent to determine whether Tadic is guilty of war crimes "in the interests of the maintenance of peace". What then? I take it that the Prosecution will answer that the Security Council is not competent to do so, is not competent to decide that Tadic is guilty of war crimes in the interests of the maintenance of peace. It would, of course, be more consistent if the Prosecutor were to be of the opinion that he nor you would be of the opinion to address this question because you are bound by the decisions of the Security Council, are you not, in the opinion of the Prosecution? We feel also in that case you may challenge the validity of such an opinion. Let us assume that we do go into the substance of the matter and wonder the Security Council in this absurd example is not competent to decide upon Tadic's guilt by exercising powers in the interests of the maintenance of peace. In that case the same question presents itself again: Where do we draw a line? This silly question necessarily implies the judgement on the powers under Chapter VII. This, your Honour, is exactly what we ask you to do, to draw a line to where the Security Council may understand its own powers and where it should not because that is far beyond what they could do. In a limited judicial review of the powers of the Security Council under Chapter VII, the relevant question seems to me to be whether a certain measure (if not mentioned explicitly by Chapter VII) does by its nature fall under Chapter VII and whether that concrete measure can reasonably contribute to the aim for which Chapter VII was drawn up. The examples given by the Prosecution of measures taken by the Security Council give a very good idea of what aims Chapter VII was meant to fulfil, measures of a political nature with possible legal consequences that aim at maintaining the peace, but not measures of a judicial nature. As I said, there are no precedents. Even though the Security Council may have the power to apply Article 39 of the Charter to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, this does not imply that Article 41 or 24 provide in a solid legal basis for the establishment of a judicial body to try war crimes. Article 41 is clearly designed to provide the Security Council with the power to impose diplomatic, financial and economic sanctions in situations involving a threat to or a breach of peace. Although the list of measures in this Article is not exhaustive, there is nothing in the text, the preparatory process, or in subsequent practice that would indicate any power on the part of the Security Council to establish the present Tribunal with its current jurisdiction. The scope of such jurisdiction is so at odds with the provisions of Article 41 that no such authority may be presumed. Article 24 of the Charter is generally recognised as containing additional powers for the Security Council to carry out its functions as a collective security organ which are not contained in specific provisions or chapters of the Charter. While such general or implied powers received some recognition in the Namibia case of the International Court of Justice, nothing in that opinion on that case would indicate that such implied powers would empower the Council to override specific limitations, or restrictions upon the Council's authority, contained elsewhere in the Charter. As has been pointed out before, the establishment of a Criminal Tribunal is not a mean which can fall under the Security Council's power to maintain that peace. An independent and above all impartial Tribunal (in the sense of the human rights treaties) is not an instrument of a political organ to influence the warring fractions. Even if the establishment of the Tribunal were to serve this purpose, we can now unfortunately (and I want to emphasise this) conclude that it has failed to serve such a purpose. The tragic events of the past few weeks confirm this in a very unpleasant way. Moreover, realistically, one might expect the leaders of the belligerent parties, being potential targets of the Tribunal and participating in the peace negotiations, not to agree to a peace settlement if they end up in the dock. It may well be the case that the Security Council will abolish the Tribunal, for the same reasons as it was established, namely, international peace and security. What is the implication of this all? This probable aspect of the dominant political foundation of the Tribunal demonstrates the lack of sufficient and consistent legal basis of the Tribunal, and brings with it the risk of it being a political instrument for the time being. Anyhow, the Security Council's actions cannot be justified by the need to act quickly. Similar arguments raised by the Prosecution might be relevant from a political and a pragmatic point of view, from a principal point of view they are irrelevant. I have pointed out before that the UN's own failure to establish a Criminal Tribunal prevents it from seeking justification in some sort of emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, before you go on to the emergency situation, let me ask you a couple of questions. I do not know how many times you have mentioned that it is political, and it may be political. The Security Council is not a judicial organ. Again, I have problems with the appropriateness of this Tribunal substituting itself for the Security Council and making a determination as to whether or not this was appropriate. Whether or not this, in fact, will deter, whether or not this will, in fact, bring about peace or maintain peace, I just do not -- I have some question about whether or not that is the proper role of a tribunal. It just seems to me that -- a judicial tribunal -- that is a factual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand your -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does that have to do with the legality?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand your hesitation to deal with these kinds of problems.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Only because I am happy that I am not a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are not we all!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am particularly happy that, as a judge, I am called upon to make judicial decisions, I am called upon to review, if we may review, the actions of the Security Council where there is some standard to guide me, and where, as judges, we can make a determination with some standards. It just seems to me that this is all kind of like jello and political considerations, and it may be political. I hope that the Tribunal does, in fact, deter, but, you know, that is for other people to decide, but I hope that we are doing a worthwhile job. The other thing is that Article 41 is not that illustrative, at least the United States amicus suggests there have been investigative commissions established. You yourself mentioned the Iraq/Kuwait Commission, but that was for civil liability. So, can you respond to those two concerns; whether or not Article 41 prohibits the establishment of a judicial tribunal, or whether what is listed is illustrative, because the language itself, I do believe, says "such as", so it indicates that it is illustrative. You are saying that some of those activities may not be of the same character as a judicial organ, and then you say that if the Security Council selects the judicial organ, they made a mistake, because it is not going to work. But I wonder whether that is something for judges to decide?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: To start with the last one, the argument is not placed in the perspective of it does not work and, therefore, you have no jurisdiction -- of course not. The argument is raised to understand that by making the decision, the Security Council should within reasonable limits be doing so within their powers. For that reason, I used this silly example of, if they understand their own powers, that it would be in the interests of peace and security to prosecute people with grey hair. Would you just accept that? Just say: "It is political; it is not our point of view. We are not going to deal with that". If they understand our own powers within the scope of the Charter and, more precisely, Chapter VII, that they can do so, that is it. We argue you cannot. You have to draw a line. The line is very difficult to describe. Elements of it are: Is there any consistency in coming to the conclusion that only people with grey hair should be prosecuted? Is there any reason to believe that the Security Council could understand such a measure within their power to maintain the peace and to address threats to peace? If you feel this is not appropriate in that meaning, then you have to come to the point I am trying to argue. So what we are saying is not a simple guidance; it is more a way of looking into the quality of the decision and to see whether it fits in a standard I cannot describe for you that is acceptable in establishing a criminal court. That standard may be of a higher level than creating an administrative court or a civil court or merely political measures with no implication for judicial organs. Here, for the first time, we deal with a decision that has been established a judicial organ that deals with criminal law. For that reason, we argue the highest standards of scrutiny should be applied. You cannot simply accept what has happened. You have to review whether this all fits in the Charter. If you come to the conclusion (as we do) that it does not fit into the Charter, then we have reached a point that the question is valid: Did the Security Council establish the Tribunal by law? Well, 41; it is not a matter of prohibiting to establish a judicial organ; the question is: Does it provide for the establishment of a judicial organ? We feel that 41 does not. Therefore, I argued that in Article 41 we cannot find any authority to do so. The authority may not be presumed. It may be presumed if it was a non-judicial organ or an organ we have to judge by lower standards, for example, an administrative organ, but if we deal with an organ provided with the right to punish, it certainly is not authorised by Article 41.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, before you proceed with your next argument, we will stand in recess until approximately 12 o'clock. (11.30 a.m.) (Short Adjournment) (12.00 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, would you continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will continue your Honour. As I have pointed out before, that the UN's own failure to establish a criminal tribunal prevents it from seeking justification in some sort of emergency situation. The Defence takes the position that there is no emergency situation, since for the crimes committed no statute of limitation applies and the trial by a tribunal established in the "normal" (that is valid) manner at a later stage cannot be excluded. Moreover, even if there were to be an emergency situation, the emergency refers to the war and the threatened peace and not to some pressing need for an immediate trial. Where the United Nations has no military instruments of its own at its disposal and it is supported militarily by the member-states, it cannot appeal to martial law, since only the member-states supplying the troops and only their judicial and military organs have a right to do so. Furthermore, it should be pointed out that expedience might possibly justify certain measures from a political point of view, an expedient and effective measure is not necessarily the same as a legal one. This problem arises, among others, in the question of how it is possible that states still are not prepared to agree on a permanent criminal court in the short term or in the foreseeable future. Apparently, no agreement can be reached on the legal basis and the powers of such a court. This difference in approach and opinion cannot be solved by a political organ like the Security Council simply establishing a criminal court itself and attributing it with jurisdiction and even primary jurisdiction over domestic courts, without the express permission to do so being given by member-states or in the Charter. One might even say it is a way of overriding the member-states. I will take up the question of whether the conflict is international more extensively when discussing the subject matter, of course. Nevertheless, what I shall say later on this issue also holds valid for this part of the Defence concerning the Security Council's powers. Despite the extensive argument put forward by the Prosecution on this matter, the key question regarding the Security Council's powers remains, in the Defence's opinion, unanswered. Where the Security Council is entitled to take measures aiming at maintaining the peace and measures to prevent a breach of the peace, one could imagine a civil war posing such a threat to spill over into other countries, that the Security Council might be competent to take measures preventing the spread of the conflict to other countries. We will certainly not dispute that. When I get to the subject matter of jurisdiction, I shall explain more in extenso that the Tadic case took place in the context of the internal Bosnian conflict between sections of the population. Regarding the position of the Security Council in this, the Defence is willing to accept that the Security Council feared the conflict on the territory of the Former Yugoslavia might spread beyond the borders and, thus, result in international conflict and, therefore, a threat to national peace. But even if that may be the case, it does not justify the establishment of an ad hoc Tribunal, since such a court -- as has been made clear by now, I hope -- can in no possible way serve to maintain or restore the peace. The appointment of the judges, I already stressed that point, has, unfortunately, not led to an end of the war or preventing war crimes from being committed. Where sanctions, military intervention (as in Kuwait/Iraq) could still be expected to serve the peace, the same thing cannot be said of the establishment of a judicial organ.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, we have not finished; the Tribunal has just begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely, but I am not to predict the future; I just make a comment on the present situation. Where the Security Council may further its humanitarian causes in its effort to maintain peace, such as, for instance, the peace-keeping operations in former Yugoslavia, that does not include a competence to try breaches of humanitarian law which, after all, do not contribute to the maintenance of peace. Finally, I will make a few remarks on the individual liability and the role played by the Security Council on this matter. Although individuals can be criminally liable for breaches of humanitarian law, individuals can, in the opinion of the Defence, not be the subjects of decisions taken by the Security Council. We feel that the Prosecution seems to have overlooked that difference. It seems somewhat exaggerated to presume that the Security Council wanted to establish a tribunal to try individuals since those individuals posed a threat to international peace. In as far as only states and not individuals are the addressees of measures taken by the Security Council, there is no reason to assume that Mr. Tadic's actions, for example, could be attributed to a certain state. My opinion, therefore, is that there are no valid arguments to assume that the Security Council was entitled to establish a judicial organ; rather the opposite may be concluded. I conclude, therefore, that the Yugoslavia Tribunal was founded without a basis in law and is not a Tribunal established by law. A trial by a tribunal that has not been established by law violates the basic human rights (as internationally recognised) of the accused. It is, therefore, the submission of the Defence that the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction in the case of Tadic, as it has not been established by law. If the Court may please, I would suggest that my colleague, Mr. Orie, will now comment on the supremacy of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With respect to action on individuals, the US amicus brief says that the Security Council has acted in the past with respect to individuals. They give as an example, I believe, where the Security Council acting under its enforcement powers under Article 39 and then adopting a measure, of course, under Article 41 have directed that individuals, for example, not engage in activities with certain countries. So, it is their position that the Security Council has done that in the past. It is also their position, the amicus at least, that if the Security Council finds that violations of international humanitarian law constitute a threat to peace, then the way to resolve that is to call upon and answer to those alleged violations of international and humanitarian law. That can only be done, you know -- in the framework of humanitarian law -- with respect to individual liability. What do you say to that? Are those other examples of the Security Council acting with respect to individuals, and how else can they act if they find that it is the violation of international humanitarian law that has constituted the threat to peace? How else can they act other than to act with respect to individuals?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: To address the first point you have raised, your Honour: The examples given in the US amicus curiae brief do refer to a different situation, as we feel, because in those cases there was in no way any judicial organ involved, nor did those measures impose any possibility of criminal offences and punishable offences. So there is some difference, because in this case the consequence of the establishment of the Court is that the Security Council accepted that only individuals may be prosecuted and not states, not organisations, whatsoever. It is individuals that are the aim of this resolution and this Statute and this Tribunal. That is quite different to the other measures where, as a consequence of measures also, individuals were addressed but not as a primary goal. That is the difference.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It just seems to me that in a sense you gave an example of, what if the Security Council made a determination that Mr. Tadic was guilty and that his actions constituted a violation of international humanitarian law, and their finding of guilt was necessary to end a threat to peace. I think that is a wonderful example, but this example that the amicus brief gives us seems to jump over a tribunal; in other words, there is nothing between what the Security Council has done and individuals in those instances, whereas, at least in this instance, there is the Tribunal then that makes this determination of guilt or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Defence accepts that, as a consequence of measures of the Security Council, individuals may be attached. I mean if you, for example, impose a sanction on a country, of course, individuals are involved, there is no doubt. In some cases we also see that individuals are even pointed out as a result of a measure which is in the normal framework of Article 43. But here we deal with a quite different position because it is not a usual measure which also has consequences for individuals; it is a measure that is only meant for individuals by creating an instrument to go for those individuals. What we argue is that within the powers of Chapter VII, the Security Council may deal with threats to the international peace by states. As a consequence of addressing such threats, you may reach for individuals, but only as a result by reaching the states. If you address the states, you have to accept that you may reach the individual too. But here the whole measure is not addressed to a state; it is creating an instrument to address individuals. For that reason, we feel it is a wholly different position, not comparable to anything that happened before. So there is no reference in previous measures that caused some direct consequence for individuals. I think that Mr. Orie will proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have not got the spelling of your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: O-R-I-E. I will talk about the primacy of the Tribunal as it has been contested by the Defence. The Defence has contested the legitimacy of attributing jurisdiction of a primary nature to the Tribunal. The issue of primacy under Article 9 of the Statute is closely related to the Ius de non evocando and the requirement that fair criminal justice should be administered by a Tribunal, established by law. If the establishment of the Tribunal is within the powers of the Security Council under Chapter VII, it has to be regarded as an emergency measure, a way out in an unacceptable situation in view of the goals to be achieved. If impunity for serious violations of international humanitarian law is to justify the establishment of the Tribunal, there should be an objective risk for such impunity whenever the Tribunal exercises its jurisdiction. The exercise of jurisdiction in any other situation would impair the rights of the accused in an unjustifiable way, since the jurisdiction of the Tribunal shows some considerable drawbacks, compared to the exercise of the domestic jurisdiction. Jurisdiction that has been established ad hoc is inferior to regular jurisdiction. Extraordinary Courts, to be understood as courts that have been established on a temporary basis to exercise jurisdiction over specific events and persons have been dealt with both in domestic constitutional law and in the law of extradition with profound suspicion as to the standards of justice to be observed. Apart from the reference to the various national Constitutions made in the Motion of the Defence, it should be emphasised that the prohibition of extraordinary courts remains in the domain of basic principles of a fair and impartial criminal justice. It is not such a vague notion as has been incorrectly suggested by the Prosecutor. Article 30, section 5, of the 1961 Constitution of Venezuela -- I am just taking an example -- which reads: "No one shall be judged by specially created tribunals or commissions, except by his regular judges and by virtue of pre-existing law", correctly situates this basic principle among the requirements of due process of law, similar to the ones explicitly, but not exhaustively, enumerated in Article 6 the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. These instruments implicitly express a similar requirement in the phrase that, in the determination of any criminal charge, the independent and impartial tribunal must be established by law. In the law of extradition a similar explicit suspicious attitude can be found. I refer to H. Schultz, Das Schweizerische Auslieferungsrecht, Swiss Extradition Law -- it is a rather old book but a very good book -- 1953, and to Kreppel Verfassungsrechtlichen Grenzen der Auslieferung und Ausweisung unter besondere Berucksichtigung der Auslieferung bei drohender Todesstrafe, a book which deals with constitutional limits in Extradition Law and Expulsion Law. But these explicitly expressed suspicions became obsolete.
