So, therefore, no longer we found such explicit expressions of the unacceptability of extraordinary courts, but it also became unnecessary to do so, while interpreting Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights in accordance with the interpretation as I just gave to you, makes it unnecessary to express this suspicious attitude. As you know, in the law of extradition the Human Rights safeguards should also be observed by the requested state by examining the risks of violations in the later stages of the criminal procedure in the requesting state.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, may I ask you a question regarding Ius de non evocando? In your brief, I believe, you said that that is a principle of international law. Is that what you said? I will see if I can find it. 7.2? Then you cite various constitutions from some countries. Are you saying that that principle prohibits the Security Council from establishing this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is perhaps the Security Council to establish an ad hoc criminal tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This principle?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: This principle, among others. The problem is that some of the constitutions have an express provision on that right to be tried by the judges that have been given to the Defendant by law. As I just explained to you, you will find it, but not explicitly, in the same way in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and in the European Convention on Human Rights. It is, I think, a generally accepted rule of criminal law and procedure, and one of my problems, of course, is that the elaboration of general principles of criminal law under international law, apart from those rules dealing with domestic jurisdiction, are not, well, since we have hardly any precedents, I must say that the development of these principles under international law are not as I would like them to be, but that is, I think, for historical reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Germany is one of the states you mentioned, provision from their constitution, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, Germany, as you know, has enacted legislation that would permit the deferral to our jurisdiction, and resulted in the transfer of Mr. Tadic to our Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will come to that point later, but just to let you know already my opinion on that issue is that if you look both at the legislation enacted by Germany, and if you look at the decision of the Supreme Court of Bavaria, then you will see that they felt that they were under an obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They may have been because of Article 24 which requires that states comply with enforcement measures of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I completely agree with you if, at least, a Statute has been a valid decision, but that is the issue I think we are discussing this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if you would care to translate the Latin tag? How would you put it in your own words, the Ius de non evocando which is not to be found in legal dictionaries, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is an old Latin term. I only can refer to how we call it in Dutch -- I can try to translate it in English because we usually use this phrase, but I would say that -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: A right to be tried by your own -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No one can be taken away from the court, from the judge, the court that has been established for these cases by law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by law, does it not? What you are really doing is saying that the Statute is not law because it was not properly enacted by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because they exceeded their powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So it comes to the same argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I am mainly talking on the primacy of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal because, you will understand, there is still a possibility that you would accept the power of the Security Council to establish an ad hoc Tribunal, but at the same time you could say that they might have exceeded their powers in giving it primary jurisdiction. So that is the main issue I am focusing on for I do not know how many minutes but for the next moments. If I may proceed? Solving the problem of concurrent jurisdiction under Article 9 of the Statute in good faith implies that no arrest warrants or mandatory request are issued for defendants facing legitimate prosecutions in the states. I was quoting O'Brien, The International Tribunal for the Violations of International Humanitarian Law in the Former Yugoslavia, in the American Journal on International Law, 1993. Dusko Tadic was prosecuted by the state of Germany without any risk of abuse of this criminal prosecution to frustrate the aims underlying the establishment of this Tribunal. Even if an individual has no standing to invoke the violation of the sovereignty of states as such, which is the claim of the Prosecutor, this does not automatically mean that violation of state sovereignty would remain without effect if the individual is directly affected by it. I would like to draw your attention to a decision of the Schweizerischer Bundesgericht -- that is the Swiss Federal Court; it is an administrative chamber dealing with extradition matters -- it is a decision of 15th July 1982, published in the Europaische Grundrechte Zeitschrift -- a German journal on human rights -- in 1983. In this decision the Swiss Court was denying extradition of a Belgium national who was lured into Switzerland by the German Police in violation of Belgian sovereignty. It denied extradition, notwithstanding a treaty obligation to extradite. I give this example just to demonstrate that even if it would be accepted that the individual has no standing to invoke the violation of sovereignty of a state, it does not mean that no conclusions or even consequences should be drawn. I come to the issue of the acceptance of this primary jurisdiction by several national authorities. The letter dated 10th August from the President of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Secretary General of the United Nations, indeed, expresses support for the establishment of an international Tribunal. But it also expresses that it does so because he looks upon the Republic and its civilian population exclusively as victims of aggression and violations of international humanitarian law. The acceptance of the formal request by Bosnia-Herzegovina for referral of Radovan Karadzic and others, it has been invoked by the Prosecutor, is hardly an argument in support of the acceptance of the primacy of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Firstly, because the exercise of domestic jurisdiction in Bosnia-Herzegovina will, clearly, remain ineffective in the present political and military circumstances. So, therefore, there will be no jurisdiction exercised, effectively, at this moment. Secondly, because of the political expediency for the acceptance of the deferral of the cases of these very persons, being known as the major political opponents of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is obvious to me. The enactment of legislation concerning the deferral procedure may have the same background as the German legislation (which I will discuss later) apart from the obvious political expediency. The Defence is not aware of any serious allegation against nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina that have been thoroughly investigated or will be prosecuted before this Tribunal. The acceptance of the primacy of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal by Germany has to be understood in the context of the presupposed legitimacy of Security Council resolutions 808 and 827, and the resulting supposedly binding obligations thereof. Therefore, the fact that Germany, as it is stated by the Prosecutor, "voluntarily" accepted the primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal just means that it has not been willing to expose itself to whatever forces (international pressure, trade restrictions), did not want to expose itself to these forces, to come to the decision that it would comply with the Tribunal's request. The German government has been confronted with these obligations to comply with a formal request for deferral by the Trial Chamber even prior to the enactment of the relevant legislation. If I look at the decision of the Trial Chamber on the application by the Prosecutor for a formal request for deferral to the competence of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia in the matter of Dusko Tadic, the decision of 8th November 1994, sub 19, it is quite clear that the Trial Chamber has confronted the German authorities with their duty to enact legislation. So, I could not say that there is this voluntariness which is presented by the Prosecutor as far as -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was not this Trial Chamber, you realise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, not this Trial Chamber; it was another Trial Chamber, but representative of the German government said they might have problems in referring the case of Mr. Tadic to the Trial Chamber because they had no legislation in order to do so, then it was clearly told to the German authorities they were under an obligation to enact this legislation. So, this makes quite clear, in my opinion, that in a situation where, of course, there was no possibility to start legal proceedings on that issue because Mr. Tadic was in prison in Munich at that time and the Tribunal would start within a few months, so I am of the opinion that the German legislative and judicial organs acted because they felt to be under an obligation to do so. You find the same kind of wordings, the same kind of expressions, both in the law regulating the co-operation with the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the law of 10th April 1995, in paragraph (1) sub I, and in the resolution of the Supreme Court of the State of Bayern of April 18th, 1995, (sub II, 2(a)), that it was felt as an obligation to do so. So this -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you for a moment? Of course, they felt under an obligation and the obligation is the Security Council action translated into the Statute. What you are saying is no more than what Mr. Wladimiroff has been saying, attacking the validity of the action taken by the Security Council as manifested by the Statute, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it comes to the down to the same basis of arguments. I am focusing on the primacy of the jurisdiction and I think Mr. Wladimiroff has discussed the powers of the Security Council to establish the Tribunal itself. I am just dealing with one of the special features of this Tribunal, but we are relying on the same basis. That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I may, if there were a provisions in these various constitutions similar to Article 39 and Article 41, and these constitutions say that a person charged with a crime shall be entitled to be tried under this international concept you spoke about, has a right to be tried by a regular court and no commissions, but if there was further in those constitutions: "But if the Executive finds that there is a threat to peace", for example, or of any kind of threat, "then measures may be taken". You see, that is what is lacking in the constitutions and what is in the Statute, in the Charter of the United Nations, this exception, so to speak. Am I making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have to read the two together. I understand that there is that principle of Ius de non evocando, but that is in the context, of course, of a national constitution which sounds very logical and fair to me that a defendant in a criminal case is entitled to be tried by a constituted court and not by one that just may be set up. But what is lacking, I imagine, in those constitutions is something akin to Article 39 and Article 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What we see is that if there is any reason to make an exception to this general rule, I think it is the constitution itself that has explicitly to make this exception. I could give you an example. For example, the Irish constitution -- I did not mention it in the papers, but you could read it from a decision of the European Court on Human Rights in the case of a certain Mr. X v. Ireland that the requirement that a court must be established by law was fulfilled in that case, because under the Irish constitution there was a special provision for these special circumstances. So, that was part of constitution itself. Perhaps it is important to go a bit deeper in the differences of regular courts and ad hoc courts which are forbidden, I think, both by Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, because part of the problems we are dealing with today are the result of, yes, the Tribunal to be established as an ad hoc Tribunal. If I look at the discussion I heard this morning about whether a court can judge upon the powers of the Security Council to establish a court, I would have liked that this discussion would not have to take place at all. That is one of the major differences between a regular courts and ad hoc courts, because there is always a reason to establish them, and it is almost always a political reason to establish them. What you are doing is you are asking a court to contribute to a political solution of a problem existing at that time. That is one of the main reasons behind the Ius de non evocando or the requirement that a Tribunal should be established by law. It is the main reason that these kinds of discussions should not occur in a court of law because it should all be arranged for on a general level. We do not have to dive into questions as to whether it is justified or not to try people with white hair, or even always to establish ad hoc courts when there is a situation when white haired people are most likely to be the defendants. I am talking about the problem of the consistency, not just in the case itself, but also on a longer range. This is a requirement which is imposed by a generally accepted rule, not only in criminal law but I think also in other fields of law, but, perhaps, more strictly in criminal law, that everyone should be equal in a criminal court. If we accept ad hoc courts, then we are accepting that sometimes there might be a group of persons that will be tried and at other moments similar groups of people might not be prosecuted. This is the main problem with ad hoc tribunals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What worries me about your argument (and I may not be understanding it) is that your attack seems to be on the ad hoc nature of this Tribunal, and yet you base it on the fact that it is not, as I understand it, established by law, because you may easily have an ad hoc tribunal established by a perfectly valid national law; what then would you say? Is it that this Tribunal is ad hoc or is it that it is not established by law because of the view you take of the Security Council's action?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that it is rather difficult now then to make a distinction between an ad hoc court and a special court, of course. Special courts are generally accepted. But one of the problems of the ad hoc court is that the idea of the establishing it comes up under the situation where there is a need for jurisdiction on this specific issue. Therefore, I think that there is even a difference between those ad hoc functioning courts, because what you find now and then is like I refer to the Irish constitution, for example, in the constitution it is said that special courts might function under special circumstances, but this means that apart from the actual situation in which the Court has to function, it has been thought over by the legislative authorities before, it has a more continuous status within the law of this country. So, I do agree with you that it is very difficult to make all distinctions, special courts, ad hoc courts, ad hoc courts with a continuous basis in the constitution or perhaps just not in the constitution but in normal legislation which might, as you know, make a difference because a constitution is more difficult to change usually. There are quite a lot of facets -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is not really the only criterion, is it established by law? You attack it by saying, no, it is not and we know some of the grounds on which you base that. But it is not whether it is special or ad hoc, it is whether it is established by law, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think you could say (and that is my opinion) that an ad hoc court is not a court which is established by law even if from a formal point of view new legislation were to be made very quickly and the ad hoc court will be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Or perhaps very slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Or perhaps very slowly ......

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It cannot be the speed of the legislature, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But I hope that you understand what I understand is the basic of this requirement, is that there is a continuous judicial organisation functioning in order to try crimes and not that specific courts are created for specific events, because then these drawbacks of these ad hoc courts become so visible, that that is the reason why both in constitutional law, but also in the law of extradition, they took this very suspicious attitude towards them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions as you are talking about Ius de non evocando, it seems to me that you are really combining two thoughts: One, sovereignty and, the other, the independence of this Tribunal. What you are saying is that this is an accepted principle in international law, and these provisions are in these various countries' constitutions, and here comes the Security Council enacting a resolution that, in a sense, because it is enacted under the enforcement provisions, the states feel compelled to comply with because they may be sanctioned. So it seems to me what you are saying is that this is an intrusion then by the Security Council into the sovereignty of states.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If that is so, the Charter provides (and I am not sure), I think it is Article 27 or, in any case, the UN Charter provides that there will be no intrusion into the domestic affairs -- this is not a direct quote -- of states except in so far as enforcement measures are taken. So, you see, there is a recognition in the Charter that there will be this intrusion, and this intrusion is permissible if it is an enforcement measure. So, it seems to me what you are really talking about is that there is this violation of sovereignty. Then you also say that because it is ad hoc and it has been this political decision and this Tribunal has been created to kind of carry out the political wishes of the Security Council and the Tribunal will try persons to advance whatever this political purpose is, even though I am not a politician, there are some attributes that politicians have and there are limitations. One of the limitations is within our Statute, and that is the Statute provides that the Prosecutor is to be independent and not receive instructions from any state. Of course, the Statute also provides that the judges are to be independent. So, it seems to me that you are combining the sovereignty notion, this intrusion into the sovereignty, which I think would be allowed and recognised by the UN Charter, so that you could put the two together and not violate Ius de non evocando, and at the same time also the independence that is provided specifically for in the Statute, it seems to me, responds to that argument. I really just want you to get it fixed for us so that we can understand what we need to do when we complete this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may recall the first lines of what I have said, that the issue of primacy under Article 9 of the Statute is closely related to the Ius de non evocando and the requirement that fair criminal justice should be administered by a Tribunal, established by law. So I do agree with you that the arguments are interrelated. Then I would like to answer your question about sovereignty. I do admit without any problem that Security Council resolutions can be of a nature that sovereignty, whether you say it would violate it or not but it will be against the sovereignty of state. But what we are talking about today is whether the Security Council establishing an ad hoc court, which might impair basically the rights of the accused -- I will come to that later -- when the Security Council does so without an explicit, I am saying, power to do so under the Charter, then, of course, it is a question of this is an enforcement measure. I do not know whether creating an Tribunal is an enforcement measure -- well, it is just the way you look upon it. I mean, what will be enforced?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exactly. That is the way the Security Council looked upon it, so are we supposed to be second guessing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Security Council was the only one that under the present Charter was able to create obligations for states. As we all know, this Tribunal could not easily function without the corporation of states. Since the co-operation was needed and since the Security Council was the only one who can impose obligations to states, it was the Security Council who had to do it. We have to understand that if I take this line of reasoning, then we know what we are in need of. We know that there is only one organ that has the power to impose obligation upon states. But whether they are competent to impose these obligations to create this Tribunal, that is the question. But there was no other organ that even could have tried to do it as the Security Council finally did. So that is my answer to your question about a sovereignty. So, I am not saying that it cannot intrude into sovereignty, but it is a question on whether there was competence to create this Tribunal, this ad hoc Tribunal, neglecting quite a lot of general principles of criminal law and procedure and then imposing these obligations upon states. When we are talking about independence, I am bit puzzled by the argument that the total independence of the Prosecutor by any state, whether this is really a sign, an indication, that now the Tribunal will be independent, because if I look at the ILC draft, we see that states can transfer jurisdiction to the Prosecutor. So, there we have exactly the opposite situation. The Prosecutor can act on behalf of the Security Council or, at least, requesting to prosecute someone under this permanent international tribunal. I cannot follow the argument that when the initiative is entirely with the Prosecutor, and if they are not dependent on states, that are independent from states because they do not receive any instructions, that that is the major feature of the independence of a tribunal, because we find a totally different situation in a tribunal which I would have preferred that is a permanent tribunal which is discussed already now for over 50 years in the UN and we at least have a draft at this moment. If I may proceed, your Honour? The response of the Prosecutor incorrectly suggests that the quotation of the Reparations Advisory Opinion is relevant for the recognition of the Bosnian Serb Republic to enjoy rights of sovereignty. I should have indicated that, but I am shifting now to a third involved state as far as the acceptance of the primacy of jurisdiction is involved. The quotation given by the Prosecutor deals with the question of whether or not international personality can be attributed to the organisation of the United Nations itself. If we look at this opinion, we see, on the contrary, that the advisory opinion makes no distinction as to whether the claim for reparation is brought (because that was the issue in the advisory opinion) against governments de jure or de facto. It is in this respect irrelevant whether the defendant state is a member of the United Nations or not. I bring to your attention that the Bosnian Serb Republic has been proclaimed prior to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and meets all the substantive requirements under customary international law to be considered as an independent sovereign state, as set out in the motion of the Defence. Recognition de jure is not a well established requirement for the existence of statehood under customary international law. The Bosnian Serb Republic has not accepted the primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal. It is the opinion of the Defence that the Prosecutor (under C sub 4 of his response) mixes up the primacy claim of jurisdiction with the principle of universal jurisdiction. A clear distinction has to be made between states transferring their sovereign right to exercise jurisdiction voluntarily to another state or combining their efforts to exercise their jurisdiction, and the compulsory imposition of a primary jurisdiction of a newly established Tribunal upon sovereign states. The Defence does not contest as such the right of individual states to exercise their jurisdiction in respect of the charges involved on the basis of the domestic acceptance of the application of this principle of universality in domestic law. The application of this principle of jurisdiction by Israel (in the Eichmann case) and by France (in the Barbie case) was the issue at stake in these cases. There is, however, no objective justification, as it has been put by the Prosecutor, to highlight the universal impact of the crimes involved, where Germany was appropriately prosecuting the defendant in this case for the crimes he is charged with. The concept of obligations erga omnes been invoked by the Prosecutor incorrectly in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you proceed with your next argument, as I indicated, we would stand in recess for lunch until 2.30, so you may pick up when we return. (1.00 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment). (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I just left behind me the arguments dealing with the acceptance of the jurisdiction of a primary nature of the Tribunal. I now come to one of the arguments raised by the Prosecutor about the concept obligations erga omnes. This concept has been invoked by the Prosecutor incorrectly. The Defence did not argue that states have no obligation and hence would be free to disregard an obligation to suppress the crimes enumerated in the Statute. We are willing to concede that the concept of obligations erga omnes has become part of existing international law, but its precise scope and significance is still highly uncertain. There is no authority to support an obligation erga omnes being implicit in the acceptance of primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal. This is especially true for states that are appropriately complying with their obligation to suppress the crimes involved. It is not the Defence that has to demonstrate the existence of an internationally accepted prohibition on the trial of criminal offences by an international trial chamber, but it is the Prosecutor who has to provide a sound and explicit legal basis for the establishment of the Tribunal, and its jurisdiction of a primary character under Chapter VII of the Charter. It can be admitted that as a rule action by the Security Council overrides the sovereign rights of states, as we discussed earlier. However, this petitio principii does not add anything to the question of the legitimacy of the action taken by the Security Council with regard to the powers attributed to it by the Charter. The Prosecutor has claimed that the exercise of primary jurisdiction does not infringe upon the rights of the accused, but the Defence has to contest this claim. As it has been set out before, the accused is exposed to jurisdiction that is the result of political decision-making. The inconsistency which seems to be acceptable in the view of the Prosecutor, the inconsistency and decision-making by the Security Council exposes the accused to arbitrariness. Nothing seems to prevent the Security Council from accepting the Tribunal to be used as a bargaining chip in future, perhaps secret, peace negotiations. This scenario for such a development has been presented to us in an intrusive way by Anthony D'Amato in his Article Peace vs Accountability in Bosnia in the American Journal of International Law 1994. It is bitter to read how the 1 United Nations might promote the peace process by dissolving the Tribunal, either by using its budgetary powers or by a resolution of the Security Council itself, thus creating an ultimate inequality among those who could expect that they will have to stand trial. The unlimited powers of Security Council in choosing their means under Chapter VII, as postulated by the Prosecutor, involves the risk of even interfering in the procedures already started before the Tribunal. No consistency is required.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean "interfering with the process already started"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If the powers of THE Security Council are absolute and if they do not have to rely upon generally accepted principles of criminal law and procedure, and if they may act inconsistent with earlier decisions, I do not see why there is any limit, at least in this view, on interference in whatever way with decisions taken earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not mean interference with decisions made by the judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps not decisions made, but perhaps interfering in the processes going on. If the Tribunal would be dissolved ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- in one day this would mean that the procedures necessarily have to be ended, or you might not even have a chance to end it because you might have lost your powers already. Apart from this risk which is inherent in ad hoc judicial organs and a major reason not to accept them, arbitrariness has to be feared in the broader sense due to the structure of decision-making in the Security Council. I will quote rather a long quote of this Article of Anthony D'Amato. "In the aftermath of Nuremberg, the very real possibility of individual responsibility for war crimes, coupled with the fact there has been no 'unconditional surrender' war since 1945, may account for the conspicuous absence of international tribunals following the Korean War, the Vietnam War, the wars involving Israel and other international conflicts. During the Persian Gulf war the idea of holding trials of Iraqi political military leaders was raised and debated in Congress, but nothing eventually came of it. Here the United Nations forces certainly had it within their powers to set up such a tribunal, and many of the Iraqi military leaders were in captivity. It may be a long time before we get documentary evidence on who decided to drop the idea of prosecuting the Iraqi war criminals. Perhaps some American military leaders feared their own prosecution for inaccuracy in the bombing of Bagdad, and thus there was little incentive to pursue the idea of a war crimes tribunal. But whatever the reasons, the failure of the international community to set up such a war crimes tribunal, when it had the means and ability to do so, must be counted as a significant negative precedent for international accountability. The conditions in Bosnia are even less favourable for war crimes tribunal than they were after the Persian Gulf war. Unlike the Iraqi military leaders responsible for war crimes in Kuwait, the persons allegedly responsible for war crimes in Bosnia are still at large and indeed are present -- or their friends are present -- at peace negotiations". It is obvious that the International Criminal Justice is impaired by the power of veto of the permanent members of the Security Council. The administration of International Criminal Justice thus becomes a toy for international politicians. I will give some more examples of how the rights of the Defence are impaired under the Statute, notwithstanding the fair trial provisions in it. This all to demonstrate why the primary jurisdiction is unjustified. It should, first of all, be pointed out that the accused, Mr. Tadic, loses his right to lodge a complaint at either the European Commission on Human Rights or the UN Committee on Human Rights concerning violation of his right to a fair trial. As you know, we are of the opinion that the requirement that the Tribunal must be established by law is one of the guarantees given by both the European Convention on Human Rights and the International Covenants on Civil and Political Rights. Both the organs I have just mentioned, European Commission and the UN Committee on Human Rights, are characterised by their independence from the judicial body that has tried the individual involved. These organs are vested with the jurisdiction to ultimately interpret the meaning of the provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. These organs, however, have no jurisdiction to review the fairness of the trial by the Tribunal. It also should be pointed out (and I must admit to you that I am very reluctant to raise this issue because of reasons which will be understandable to you) that the inappropriate remuneration of Defence counsel is due to insufficient funding of the Tribunal by the United Nations, thus not enabling the accused, and accused persons in the future, to properly prepare their defence. The remuneration covers far less than 50 per cent of the real office costs -- I am not talking about fees; just about the office costs -- of an average law firm. It further causes considerable restrictions on experts to be hired by the Defence (limited to 500 Dutch guilders which is approximately $300 for the case). The requirement of getting free legal assistance by counsel for those who cannot afford it is thus impaired by a significant inequality of arms. The European Commission on Human Rights has ruled that the right to counsel should be effective. I would suggest to you that I pass to my colleague, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have two questions or, perhaps, comments; the first relates to the inability of Mr. Tadic to raise a claim before the International Court of Human Rights. Even if the Tribunal had been established by the General Assembly or by treaty, would he be able to then raise claims that he was denied certain rights before the European Court of Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It would depend on the recognition of the jurisdiction of these organs, so it is rather difficult for me to explain whether these organs ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Neither would the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- would be competent because I do not know any Statute, I only know the ILC draft. But especially because most of -- I do agree with you -- of the human rights in criminal procedure in the Statute have been copied from the European Convention on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. One of the things that is not copied is the requirement that the Court should be established by law and, as I explained this morning, we would have far less problems with this specific part of the human rights granted to the accused if there would be a permanent tribunal. It is one of issues that is only likely to be raised especially ad hoc Tribunals. So I do agree with you that this might not have been different if this ad hoc Tribunal would have been established by the General Assembly, apart from I am not quite sure whether this would be possible or not, and it would have been established by treaty, then, of course, it depends on the on content of the treaty whether or not the European Convention on Human Rights would be applicable, and whether the jurisdiction of the European Commission on Human Rights, later on the European Court of Human Rights, would be accepted or not. It is not impossible to accept the applicability of the European Convention of Human Rights for international organisations. So, for example, the European Union has accepted the European Convention of Human Rights as binding, so that would be a possibility if the Tribunal would have been established under a treaty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we really do not know at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The other question has to do with remuneration. Do not be reluctant to raise anything, I suppose, but let me suggest that if that is your position, that the fees that are available affect the accused's rights to effective representation, I would suggest that you bring that to the attention of the Tribunal in the form of an official motion as opposed to just making passing reference to it. I was a judge in the United States, and I have never really heard a lawyer tell me, and when I was in practice also, I was never really satisfied with the remuneration that I got from appointments -- I did not get too many appointments, thank goodness -- but I have never heard any lawyer say that they are really what he or she deserves. But, if that is the situation, please bring it to the attention of the court in a formal motion, and we will always -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You mean within this case?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Within this case, if you wish. Certainly, if it is your position that it affects Mr. Tadic's right to adequate representation, yes, you should bring it to the court in the form of a motion or, if you prefer, write a letter. Tell us what you think. After we have resolved this issue, we will do that because it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We will not resolve that at this moment, but we will follow that pattern that by filing a motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think Mr. Vujin will make a statement before I will take -----

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like only to supplement the representation of Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask the spelling of your name?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: M-I-L-A-N V-U-J-I-N, but also I would like to do it in the language of the Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe the request was made prior to this hearing -- is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the establishment of the International Criminal Tribunal for persons responsible for crimes committed on the territory of the Former Yugoslavia upon the resolution of the Security Council, we consider it is not established according to the international law. The provision No. 29 of the Charter of the UN cannot be a legal foundation for the establishment of the Tribunal, because the provision No. 29 does not envisage that the Security Council could establish an international Tribunal. According to the Article 29, it is envisaged that the Security Council could establish some supplementary additional organs that it esteems to be needed to fulfil its tasks. So, my question is as follows: Can the ICTY be an additional organ of the Security Council? The answer of the Defence is, no. No international criminal tribunal can be considered as an additional organ of some other body. A tribunal is a court and it should be established according to the international law or the internal national law of some state. A UN Security Council is a political and executive body of the organisation of the United Nations, and it does not have a competence, a power, to establish a court, a tribunal, let alone a tribunal that should be in charge of such serious crimes. The decision based on the Article No. 29, we consider this to be a political decision, a decision that has managed to exert a certain political pressure and not a decision based on law. This decision represents a legal absurd. I would like to ask you the following question: If the Security Council, as a political and executive organ of the UN, decides to establish a tribunal and, according to the Article 29, it is allowed to establish only additional organs, what kind of help does it provide in peace keeping? What is the Tribunal meant to do in such a case? A Tribunal should establish whether some one is guilty or not according to the international rules. The Tribunal is not here to help any executive body. If this Tribunal were established by the decision of the General Assembly of the United Nations, according to some convention that would have been agreed upon by other states, then we should be in a position to discuss about the role of the Tribunal. But in this case, the decision was taken by a small organ represented by a very small number of countries. Other states were not consulted at all whether the Tribunal should be established or not. There is another question that seems to be very important. This Tribunal was created in order to prosecute those who are responsible for the crimes committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991. According to the International Conventions, there is no prescription for war crimes, but what will happen with other war crimes, we have to ask ourselves, where other war crimes committed elsewhere in the world, should someone be held responsible for those crimes? No executive body can decide to establish a Tribunal so that this Tribunal could help it to keep the peace in the world. This Tribunal, through Tadic's trial, will not be able to help in peace keeping. This is, your Honour, what I wanted to add to Mr. Wladimiroff's and Mr. Orie's explanations. Now I will continue in English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, if I may, in the form of a question. Am I correct that many countries, more than the number on the Security Council, had input with respect to the establishment of this Tribunal? When I say "input", they commented on the establishment, either supporting it, or suggesting that it be established by way of a convention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, I mean, there was an opportunity, I gather, then for member-states to at least speak to the appropriateness, from their point of view, of the establishment of the Tribunal by the Security Council; is that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: As you may know, your Honour, some countries did express such views. Some countries did have objections on the establishment of the Tribunal, but, you know, it is one thing to give its theoretical, practical or other views on certain issues, but it is something completely different when you are asked to take part in a decision making on the establishment of some organ or body. So the question is whether we can accept such a decision or no. With regard to this, I would like to mention the issue that was raised by you, your Honour, and it is related to the decision of the German authorities to change their law in order to be able to recognise this Tribunal. The Germans did do it, but in such a way that they could surrender to this Tribunal, or to some other Tribunal, citizens that are not German citizens and this is not a way to recognise this Tribunal. Germany would not have accepted to surrender its own nationals to this Tribunal. Can I continue in English? I would like to state some facts, historical and other, which show that the conflicts in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina are not international, they are internal. In mid-tenth century, Bosnia was mentioned for the first time in Constantine Porphyrogenitus "de administrando imperio", as an area within Serbia. At that time Bosnia was the region around the geographical designations within the Serbian state rather than a separate state entity. The section subtitled "of the Serbs and of the Country they now dwell in" clearly shows that Serbs settled in Bosnia as early as the ninth century, i.e. that the Bosnia has been a Serb land. In the 12th century Pope Urban the Third regards Serbia and Bosnia as identical and speaks about the political and ecclesiastical unity of these lands. The Pope likewise confirms the rights of the Dubrovnik Church by 1187 Charter in which he says: "Regnum Seruilie, quod est Bosna... - Kingdom of Serbia -- that is Bosnia". John Kinnamos refers in his article "Campaign on the Tara in 1150" to the Drina River which separates Bosnia from the rest of Serbia, meaning to say that even then Serbs were living in Bosnia. In the 12th century Priest Dukljanin also says that the Drina River separates Serbia into two regions - Bosnia and Raska. Bosnia rulers in the 13th and 14th centuries exclusively designated their subjects as Serbs and referred to Serbian as the only language in Bosnia. The charters of the Bosnian Governor, Matija Ninoslav, 1249 used the term "Serb" to denote an inhabitant of Bosnia and the Charter of Governor, Stjepan Second Kotromanic, addressed to Dubrovnik regarding the sale of Rati in Ston, dated March 1333, notes that "two of the charters are Latin and two are Serb". The Cyrillic, as the Serbian script, was used in Bosnia from the earliest times. The Charter of Kulin Ban, issued to the people of Dubrovnik in 1189 was also written in it. It was used later on too in the offices of the Bosnian rulers and feudal lords as well as in church books. From the beginning of the 15th century external political circumstances began to change and Bosnia was being increasingly attacked by Turks. Their attacks forced King Tvrtko the Second to become a vasal both to the Hungarian king and to the Turkish Sultan, to whom he paid regular yearly tributes, as of 1415. Bosnia finally fell under Turkish rule in 1463. The Turks abducted Serb boys, took them to the centres of the Ottoman Empire where they were Islamized and trained for soldiers - notorious janissaries. There was constant religious intolerance. As of 1767 the Serbs lost their autocephalous Church and were officially considered "Romaics". In 1853 a Turkish regulation was enacted banning the use of the Serbian name. From 1868 the rule was introduced that in national terms the entire population had to declare themselves as being Osmanli. After the Serb uprising in 1874 which broke out as a result of terror, 250,000 Serbs or one fourth of the total population crossed the Bosnian border into the Hapsburg-ruled lands. Later on, another 80,000 Serbs fled Bosnia and moved into Serbia and Montenegro. The first official population census in 1879 showed that the proportion of the three religious communities was: Serbs, 43 per cent, Muslims 38 per cent, Catholics 18 per cent and others one per cent. The execution by firing squads of 84 Serbian peasants at the hand of the Muslim volunteers Schutzkorps in Celebici on the River Drina, at the outset of the World War I, presaged genocide and large scale massacres that were to follow. The violence to which the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been subjected in 1914 was the reason why it was only there that some previous democratic institutions were not restored. Parliaments which have been disbanded in 1914 their renewed in all countries of Europe. This was not done in Bosnia-Herzegovina lest the Serbs demanded investigations of the crimes committed. Instead, the Governor of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Sarkotic, made plans for Bosnia-Herzegovina to become part of Greater Croatia for the establishment of an alliance of Croats and Muslims, in which way the unification of Yugoslavia around Serbia would be precluded. The national question of Serbs, but also of the other South Slav nations - Croat and Slovenes - was resolved with the creation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918. This kingdom was formed when the kingdom of Montenegro entered territories which have belonged to the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy before World War I, and inhabited by Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, joined the kingdom of Serbs. The unification was achieved on the basis of the right of peoples to self-determination which was then valid as a political prison. The Muslims in the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes were protected as a religious minority. Their status was governed by Article 10 of the Treaty which the principal allied and associated powers and the state of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes signed in St. Germain-en-Lais on 10th September 1919. Article 10 of this Treaty reads: "The Serb-Croat-Slovene State agrees to grant to the Muslims in the matter of family law and personal status provisions suitable for regulating these matters in accordance with the Muslim usage. The Serb-Croat-Slovene State shall take measures to assure the nomination of the Reiss-u-Ulema". The above facts are showing clearly that Muslims, until the Constitution of 1974 was passed, were a religious minority. In accordance with Article 1 of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the status of Muslims improved from that of religious minority to that of a people, and it reads as follows: "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a Socialist, democratic state and a socialist self-managed democratic community of the working people and citizens, the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina - Muslims, Serbs and Croats and persons belonging to the other peoples and nationalities living in it, based on the rule and self-management of the working class and all working people and on the sovereignty and equal rights of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of persons of other peoples and nationalities living in it." "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia". This is a probably a unique case in the history of the world that a religious community was advanced to the status of a nation. Historically speaking, Serbs have been living for centuries in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all the conflicts which have or are occurring are having the character of a civil war, because the parliament of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted the constitution of the Bosnia Serb Republic on 28th February 1992. The Bosnian Serb Republic founded its Army on 13th May 1992. That dates before the beginning of the conflicts in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, would you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: All these dates are before the beginning of the conflict in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The conflict -- are you saying -----

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Army conflict in Prijedor, that is all. All army conflicts in the Prijedor area, where live Mr. Tadic, was between Muslims and Serbs. They live in -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In May, the Yugoslav Army, the JNA ---

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- left in May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes. On 19th May, the Former Yugoslav National Army, 19th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They left?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: They left.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before, they were in that area, in that country -- in that area that later became recognised as a country in June or was it April? So they left. So you are saying that this is not an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Not international character, that is internal character.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 39, though, of the UN Charter does the Security Council not have the authority to declare that there is a threat of peace, that the activities constitute a threat to peace, need the activities be international in character?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Only the conflict with international character can establish the peace in the war.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that you are saying that the Security Council does not have authority under Article 39 ---

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- to then take a measure under Article 41, unless the character of the conflict is international?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are aware that the United Nations, the Security Council, has taken action with respect to other alleged internal conflicts, for example, Rwanda, and they have taken action under Article 39, Article 41, but you would say that is illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff, do you wish to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, please. Your Honour, before going into the matter, the subject matter, of jurisdiction, I want to clarify maybe some things that have been said in the previous discussion. The subject I am going to discuss will also deal with the issue of internal or international conflict, armed conflict. I will discuss this matter in the context of the Geneva Treaty, Convention, and The Hague Convention, of course, and the other relevant conventions I will refer to. I will not discuss the matter within the context of Article 31 of the Charter -- I think you will appreciate that -- because that is a quite different issue that has to do with the question whether the Security Council is able to assess that some conflict may be a threat, though being internal, to the international peace. Let me phrase it in this way. In that respect, being it internal, international, it is not relevant for the matter I am going to discuss.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I was just asking Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, that is the reason why I just make this statement. Then, the final point concerning the jurisdiction to be raised by the Defence concerns the subject matter jurisdiction, as laid down in Articles 2 to 5 of the Statute and, in fact, we are dealing with Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the Statute. What I will do is discuss Article 2 and then separately Article 3 and then separately Article 5. Then I will try to bring it altogether. When I start with Article 2 of the Statute, I think the Prosecution and the Defence do not disagree in their interpretation of Article 2 referring to grave breaches of the Geneva Convention, and not to any of the grave breaches under Protocol 1 to this convention. We do disagree, however, with the Prosecution how far -- let us put it this way, we do agree on the question whether the grave breaches of the Geneva Convention IV applies in the case of Dusko Tadic. To repeat it, we do not agree, as I see it, in the interpretation of Article 2 of the Statute referring to grave breaches of Article 147 of the Geneva Convention, but not referring to Protocol 1 of the Convention, that the issue is we disagree about the applicability of the grave breaches, not where we can find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, would you mind repeating that? I have not fully understood what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. The Prosecution and the Defence, as we see it, do not disagree in their interpretation of Article 2 of the Statute referring to grave breaches of Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV, and not referring to any of the grave breaches under protocol 1 of this convention. We do agree (sic), however, on the question whether Article 147 of the Geneva Convention applies in the case of Dusko Tadic -- we disagree, yes, of course. I am sorry, I am mixing those all up. If I refer to 147 of the Convention, I mean the grave breaches. This difference in opinion concerns two issues. First, whether there was an internal or an international armed conflict at the relevant time and, second, whether Article 147 has been brought into force by a special agreement between the parties concerned. I think these are the two issues we are going to deal with. From a number of perspectives, the Prosecution replies in the affirmative to the first question: Yes, do they say, this would amount to an international armed conflict and, therefore, the grave breaches are applicable. In our motion and brief following it, I have replied to this question negatively. We maintain the position that the armed conflict on the territory of Bosnia -- I am not referring to the territory of the Former Yugoslavia -- was an internal conflict. I will now elaborate that issue. No further argument, I hope, is needed to understand that the question of whether the provision concerning the grave breaches applies in relation to the jurisdiction is a legal question. I think there is no doubt about. It is the Tribunal's judicial duty to examine this question independently of what others might think. The answer to this legal question depends, as indicated earlier, in the first place upon the question of whether there was a "declared war or any other armed conflict between two or more of the Higher Contracting Parties" as meant in Article 2 of the Geneva Convention IV.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The US amicus takes the position that the grave breaches would apply even if it was internal. You are responding to that point today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will pass that point. As I have argued in great detail early on, the Defence suggests that the Trial Chamber is not bound by the opinion of the Security Council or any other organ of the United Nations on this question, this legal question. The Security Council's characterisation of the conflict may give some indication and the resolutions of the General Assembly may carry some weight, but these opinions certainly do not legally bind the Tribunal. It is your own free independent assessment. The United Nations' opinion on the status of the conflict is a political judgement of the facts which are known up till then and certainly not a legal-technical assessment of the application of Article 2 of the Geneva Convention IV. Moreover, it should be considered that these opinions of the United Nations organs are formulated with an entirely different aim in mind from that of the Tribunal (namely to address presumed threats to international peace and security rather than administering justice to an accused). So we suggest that the expose given by the prosecution of the different opinions voiced by various organs of the United Nations are not significant. They may carry some weight but they do not define the question we put forward. The same applies for the submission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the International Court of Justice quoted by the Prosecution, in as far as this submission might be understood as an implicit acceptance of the conflict as being international. The Prosecution's interpretation of this submission is, in fact, incorrect since the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia does certainly not recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state. It is for this very reason that the submission speaks of "the authorities under the control of A. Izetbegovic". I suggest that this position of the Prosecution lacks all basis in fact, not in the last place as it is generally known that precisely this principle of not recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is one of the key issues of the whole Yugoslavia problem at this moment. So it is a well-known fact and I will not elaborate on that furthermore. In this respect, I would like to point out that words "From the moment Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state" and so on, as mentioned in paragraph 5.1 of our brief, and marked by mistake by the Prosecution in its response as 5.6, refer to an objective assessment of the fact and do not in any way express the Defence's subjective opinion. I am quite willing to accept my formulation might not have been in perfect English and can, therefore, have given rise to confusion, but I stipulate again it is an international accepted fact that states have recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Defence does not pertain any position on that matter. However that may be, during the relevant period of May - August 1992, and now I will make some remarks about historical facts of very recent date -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can ask you, how is this Tribunal, this Chamber, to deal with these questions? Are they to take judicial notice of dates, facts, withdrawal of the Yugoslav Army and non-withdrawal, facts that may make all the difference between a clearly international conflict and one that is internal, or are they to defer this whole issue until there is evidence (if there is going to be evidence) before the Chamber concerning those facts? What is your submission on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is a very interesting issue you are raising because, indeed, I may try to give you some guidelines how to view this subject matter jurisdiction issue but, on the other hand, it is hard to understand how you can do that without establishing facts. You need some fact. I will try to explain this later why some dates may be of vital importance. You can deal with that by two ways. What I have tried to do is to rely on facts that are public, and known public documents, and which as a fact as such are not disputed. I may make some commentaries try on it and they may be disputed by the Prosecution, but I rely on facts which I think are not disputed. If you feel, after hearing the Prosecution, that the facts as such, a date, what happened, is not disputed, then you may proceed by yourselves. At the moment we find ourselves in a dispute about the facts, then indeed we face a problem. We might deal with that in two ways. One way has already been suggested by the Prosecution, I think, that it is the advisory opinion of Mr. Gow, as far as I remember. It has not yet been produced, but we might discuss the matter whether you will produce it and we may produce on our side a report on the facts too, and then it is for your chamber to proceed. I am not ready to say we are going to do that, but this option I have in consideration because you have already prepared such a expert witness statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is attached to Professor Gow, I guess it is? That is attached to the Prosecutor's submission, I do believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us see where we are when we hear your argument and the Prosecutor's argument. Maybe there is a possibility that stipulations can be made between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then some matters we can take judicial notice of, resolutions, for example, of the Security Council, but you will tell us at some point, will you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will try to get through this mess. To starts with, we feel that the relevant period is May- August 1992 because that is the period of the indictment. In that period of time, Bosnia had already seceded from the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and had been recognised by a number of states as an independent state, though not by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I think there is no dispute about these facts. I recall that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has not recognised Bosnia and as an independent state either. That may be disputed, but I think it is a fact. I would like to return to the question of the status of the conflict and suggest that the conflict on the territory of the former Yugoslavia is not only complicated but has a multiple character into the bargain. It cannot simply be characterised as only international or only internal. Now I refer to the whole territory of the former Yugoslavia. If you view the whole territory, you cannot simply say it is all internal or international. Of the whole period, the conflicts on the territory of the former Yugoslavia have been alternatively depending on time and place of an internal and/or international nature. In the Defence's opinion the status of the conflict should not be judged in such a general view -- that is the whole territory of the Yugoslavia -- but against the background of the case against Tadic, which would limit our scope to what is relevant in the case of Tadic. It concerns conduct that, if proven, can only fall within the jurisdiction under Article 2 of the Statute in a certain context. So we depend on the context. This jurisdiction can only arise if the conduct of which Mr. Tadic is accused has taken place on those places and in those times mentioned in the indictment in the context of an international armed conflict. If not, there will be the answer to the question which has been raised when I started this part of our plea. We, therefore, suggest that in order to determine the status of the conflict, what is relevant, is not the situation on the entire territory of former Yugoslavia, but only the status of conflict in the Opstina of Prijedor, that is, the town and soundings of Prijedor. We also suggest that in order to determine the status of the conflict one should not take into account the whole period from the beginning, that is say, 1991, up to now, but only the status of the conflict in the period from 27th May until 3rd August 1992. I will explain that. If you look into paragraph 3.5 of the indictment, you will find it refers to the period of 24th May to 30th August, but it has also been stipulated in that paragraph that this period only applies "unless otherwise set forth below (in this indictment)". So we have to look at the charges to find the earliest date and to find the last date. You will see that the earliest date you will find is 27th May and not 24th May if you look into charge No. 10. The latest date you will find is not 30th August 1992, but it is 3rd August in connection with charge 4. So what we find here in the indictment is that the relevant period is not the period from 24th May to 30th August, but the period from 27th May until 3rd August 1992. That is, in our view, the limited period we have to consider if we have to assess what was the status of the conflict in that period in this area and was it an internal or an international one.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, then if a foreign country invaded or intruded Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to that time and then withdrew before this period of time, this May 27th, then are you saying it may have been international before but upon withdrawing the conflict is converted to an internal one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Exactly. I will try to elaborate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Really, it is more complex than that, because if they withdraw from portion but not from the whole, you have an internal conflict, perhaps, within that portion, but an international one. So you have both spatial and temporal concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is left, you have to consider what they did, and if it was not in the area where Mr. Tadic lived and the offence occurred, then it might be not be relevant for the offence in that area, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is a concept of extraordinary artificiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are dealing with the defence, your Honour. These criteria, limited in time and place, of commission of the alleged offences will make clear immediately that in its response the Prosecution has assumed a point of reference which is far too broad (both in time and in place). In the Defence opinion the events which took place on the territory of the former regional republic of Bosnia before and after the secession from the Federal Republic on 6th March 1992, have not developed unambiguously. We believe that the regional republic of Bosnia has been torn apart, politically speaking, by political factions, organised on the basis of ethnic background, before the formal secession from the federation became effect.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, I think Mr. Tadic is having difficulties. Can you hear, Mr. Tadic? Mr. Tadic, can you hear me? Yes. Mr. Wladimiroff, you speak in your microphone and make sure he can still hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Okay, I will continue, your Honour. We believe that the regional republic of Bosnia had been torn apart, politically speaking, by political factions, organised on the basis of ethnic background, before the formal secession from the Federal Republic became a fact. We suggest that the desire of many Serbs living in the regional republic of Bosnia not to secede from the Federal Republic, apart from the Croatian problems, is one the reasons that the events in the regional republic of Bosnia did not develop unambiguously, before the secession from the federation. The reaction of the government of the regional republic of Bosnia and the formation of a Bosnian Serb government exercising authority of a part of the territory are parts of these events. This secession (by the Bosnian Serbs) has until now not been recognised by states who later were to recognise the former regional republic of Bosnia as an independent state. We also suggest that the secession of the regional republic of Bosnia from the federation on 6th March 1992 is one of the primary reasons that the events in the former regional republic did not develop ambiguously. The premature recognition thereafter on 7th April 1992 of Bosnia as an independent state by several states only strengthened these developments. We do not deny that the activities of the Yugoslav National Army, JNA, up to the moment of its retreat from the regional republic of Bosnia on 19th May 1992, did also play a role in the developments. I think these are fair facts just in simple words what happened up to that date. Then, it is a fact that in the areas where almost the entire population is from the same ethnic background there was a certain coherence. As far as this concerned related areas of a predominant Muslim background, the developments which led to an armed conflict became of a more external character. In the areas in which (and I hope I am clear about this) the Muslim government was, in fact, in control, the relationship described by the Prosecution between the Yugoslav National Army and the forces of the Muslim government plays an important role. As far as the role played by the Yugoslav National Army is concerned, I will confine myself to pointing out that their role is not unambiguous and that the Defence does not agree with the description of that role given by the Prosecution. But for reasons mentioned on later, the role of the Yugoslav National Army is irrelevant to the legal question now being discussed. Why? I will try to explain this. I may draw your attention to the distinction between the Yugoslav National Army, directed by the Federal Secretariat for Peoples Defence in Beograd, and the Territorial Defence Force, an irregular force, directed by the secretariats of each republic. At the end of the 80s the system of new military district resulted in the increased autonomy of superior JNA command. So we are dealing here with two entities, the JNA, central command and local forces with a decentralised command. What happened on May 19th 1992? On that date, the JNA was split up in two entities. The Yugoslav Army, it was not named any more the Yugoslav National Army, but it changed its name into the Yugoslavia army, was withdrawn from Bosnia, and the remaining part, may I refer to it "Bosnian Army", was the remaining part on the territory. Well, what happened? The Bosnian Army was composed of Muslims, Serbs and Croats who, in fact, proceeded later on as separate armed groups. They fell apart. It was possible because there were local forces so they melted together each by ethnic determination. That is what happened in the assessment of the Defence up to the period up to 19th May 1992. But however it may be -- we will hear later what the Prosecution will say about this -- as far as the relationship between the JNA -- I am talking before the 19th -- and the forces controlled by the Muslim government has led to exchanges of armed conflicts in those parts of Bosnia before the JNA being retreated from Bosnia. I have no doubt that these conflicts may be characterised as armed conflicts of international character. There were clashes. We do not dispute that. The declaration of a state of war by Bosnia on 22nd June 1992 (which declaration was probably motivated more by politics, than being the expression of a real situation of, whatever it may be) did not affect other parts of the territory than those under the control of the Muslim government. We have to realise that. Tadic never lived in those areas. Tadic never lived in those areas which have been under control of the Muslim government. The conduct of which Mr. Tadic is accused has not taken place in those areas. We suggest that in the areas with a predominantly Serbian population, the role of the JNA has not led to any armed conflict and certainly not to a conflict with forces controlled by the Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You are talking about now before 19th May?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Before and after.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that after May 19th, 1992, when the JNA retreated from Bosnia-Herzegovina and they did not leave behind the equipment forces who became a part of an army that continued to battle with Bosnia-Herzegovina army in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I am saying is that if you split up the Yugoslav National Army into two armies, the Yugoslav Army withdrawing and the other part being for a very short period a "Bosnian Army", split up in three parts, of course, those elements and parts that remained had access to what was left to them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So each took their own part of the barracks, the equipment, the weapons. Of course, there maybe a difference in who got what and who had any advantage but, as a matter of fact, it was a split up.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So the Croatians who were a part of the army that was left took some, Muslims took some and Serbs took some?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And that was normal because they had already a framework of this national territorial army. In that framework each picked out what they thought they needed. What we suggest is that when after the 18th or 19th clashes may have occurred between those groups controlled by the Muslim government and the withdrawing JNA, clashes occurred not in the area where Tadic lived. It occurred in areas where the Muslim government had control over its own territory, but it did not occur in the Opstina of Prijedor. So we say that if such clashes might be of an international character, it happened elsewhere in Bosnia, but not in the area where Tadic lived because there was no involvement of the JNA whatsoever and there were not any clashes between any troop controlled by Muslim government. It was another situation. We suggest that in the areas with a predominantly Serbian population the role of JNA has not led to armed conflict with forces controlled by the Muslim government. That happened elsewhere. What happened in these areas with the predominantly Serbian populations? The JNA withdrawn, left their equipment and weapons behind to this new force which was a part of the Bosnian force but turned out to be a Serbian force. But no clashes between the JNA and Muslim troops because there was no conflict in that area. The Opstina of Prijedor was after 30th April 1992 -- you will find this also with Professor Gow's report -- and still is a Serbian held territory, and we suggest that in this Opstina no armed conflicts have taken place between forces of the Muslim government and the JNA. So in this area no armed conflicts have taken place of an external nature. That brings us to the question, where there conflicts? Yes, there were. I will now focus on the areas with a mixed population.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Were there conflicts in that area, the Prijedor area, after May 19th, 1992, between Serbian forces that took a share of the JNA's equipment and then continued to operate but under a Serbian army name?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right. They took over in villages, towns, and then we see all this, what we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They were then in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
