utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fighting with Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They were taking over villages like Prijedor; there was a lot of shooting and people were taken away and detained in camps for the mere fact they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That area was controlled by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: By the Serbian Bosnian Republic and by the Serbian Army. No JNA, no Muslim troops, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But they have the remnants of the equipment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Of course. The Serbs had, the Muslims had and the Croats had. It was logical because originally they had nothing. They had only a structure, the territorial army. Then in this structure was fit in the remaining part of JNA that was in Bosnia. If we now focus on the areas with the mixed population, then we can conclude that conflicts and riots between the different population groups have taken place. Leaving the Croatian problems we can roughly distinguish two situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you go on, may I explore this question of the spatial jurisdiction of the Geneva Convention's provisions or certain of them? If you are in an area where there was clearly an international conflict you take prisoners, then if you move them to an area where there is no such conflict the grave breaches would not apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not prepared to say no. I have to give it a thought. It seems to me that if causal relations are ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So it may continue to attach because prisoners were captured in an area where there was at that time international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It seems to me that if the origin of the action that covers part of the grave breech will become a grave breach later on if you take into account what happened elsewhere, it may be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Likewise as far as the temporal aspect is concerned: If somebody is taken prisoner at a time when there is an international conflict, the grave breaches provision continues to apply to him or her after the end of that conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That may be the case, but it is not ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But you say this is not the case here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is not relevant here. I understand what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is testing curiosities of the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. There are a lot of questions we cannot deal which are highly interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: They may also be highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, if there is a causal relation, that is what happens in the relevant period was exclusive result of previous events, and therefore is a causal relation. What I tried to argue is that there is no logical relation in the context of the Geneva Convention with what happened elsewhere in Bosnia and what happened in the area where Mr. Tadic lived. They may have occurred at the same time, but we have to establish a logical relation; for example, the one was taken prisoner in that area where an international conflict was going on and taken to the area of Mr. Tadic. Indeed you have a relation, but that is not our case. All the offences happened in the Opstina of Prijedor. It is a very closed area. I have been there, I have seen it. It is a closed area and for that reason it is very understandable that, well, everyone knew what was going on behind the mountains, but does it mean that what happened there has a causal relation to what happened in the Opstina Prijedor? In the political sense it does, but in the context of the Geneva Convention then we need more I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It also must follow that if in the same camp there were some who came from an area where they had been originally taken either at a time, well, at a time when there was international conflict, to them the grave breaches would apply in that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the Prosecution is able to establish that the persons involved in the indictment have been brought in from outside ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- where an international conflict occurred, it may be the case. I will give that a thought. I am not prepare to say it will. It seems to me there is no evidence whatsoever to establish such a ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am not suggesting that you ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No. I understand. It is just theoretical.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, as to whether the JNA left behind equipment, and perhaps even troops, that then began to operate under the banner of the Bosnian Serbs when they withdrew on May 19th, whether or not they left behind that equipment for Serbs and not for Croats and Muslims, may be one of the questions that we will have factual problems. The Prosecutor of course do not take the position that it was divided equally. They take the position that everything was left for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am prepared to accept that it was not equal. I have no evidence to judge it, but for the argument sake I will accept that it might not have been equal. But is it relevant for the determination of being an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why is it not relevant? If the JNA left in name only and continued to operate but under ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is more between zero and inequality of equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is more between leaving nothing and an equal part.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand on equal. I am saying if in fact they left just in name only and then basically turned over everything to the Bosnian Serbs, which may be the position of the Prosecutor, that is the way I read it, and thereafter the JNA was operating not under their name but basically through the Bosnian Serbs. That may be a very difficult fact question for us to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But as to declaration of war, what you are saying is when Bosnia-Herzegovina declared a war against Serbia in June 1992 they could only speak for that territory over which they had control. If they did not have control over Prijedor then they could not say that the Prijedor area was in a state of war with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is exactly what I am arguing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That I understand. That may be a little easier for us to get hold of in terms of some kind evidence that is in the form of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Anyhow, I do see it a problem of establishing facts on the basis on you have to assess what was going on in terms of was it an international or internal conflict, but let me proceed. I was talking about areas with a mixed population. I said you may make a distinction between two types. As far as areas are concerned controlled by the Muslim government, inhabited by small concentrations of Serbs, if I can be short, the Opstina of Prijedor was not in such an area. It was not controlled by the Muslim government and there was not a small concentration of Serbs. It was just the other way round. We have as the remaining areas, areas in the control of the Bosnian Serb government with small concentrations of Muslims. That indeed was the case in the Opstina of Prijedor. There were indeed small concentrations of Muslims in this area. We suggest that in this Opstina the conflict expressed itself in different ways: Armed action by the Bosnian Serb government troops, and conflicts, whether armed or not, ethnically different persons being disorganised or maybe organised or militia of just armed civilians. So we have to distinguish between two groups. I repeat that: Bosnian Serb government troops taking over in places, in villages, in towns, and on the other hand conflicts, whether armed or not, between persons of different ethnical descent; they were organised, they were not organised, in some parts the militia took a part in it and at other times just armed civilians. We also suggest that the acts of violence which took place there in this Opstina, took place entirely within the area under the control of the Bosnian Serb government. There was no control by the Muslim government; no control by the Croat government. It was in the heart of the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb government.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: From May through to August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When did the Bosnian Serb government declare itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: On two occasions, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In May or later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, they declared it in January 1992 and reconfirmed that on April 7th, 1992. Reconfirmation had to do with the change of name. The first declaration was -- I say this by heart -- the 27th -- I may give you the exact date in a minute -- that was on 9th January 1992 in the name of the Bosnian Serbian Republic. Apart from the question whether this government, the Bosnian Serb government, or the Serb Republic government is recognised or not. It is important to point out that, therefore, the conflict in the Opstina of Prijedor is not of an external nature. In the area of any troop under Muslim control, there was no one in the area, no troops under JNA control. They had already withdrawn. The problems of not withdrawing was in the Muslim area. If you now place these developments in time, then it is the Defence opinion that the events in the period from 27th of May until 3rd August 1992 were of an exclusive internal character. It all happened in the area without anyone from abroad. Viewed from this perspective, it cannot be claimed that the conduct of Mr. Tadic occurred in relation to an international armed conflict, in the meaning of Article 2 of the Geneva Convention IV. This opinion remains unaltered by the fact that the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a contracting party to the Geneva Convention IV, or by the facts that the Muslim government considers itself as a successor of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on its own territory at 31st December 1992 and retroactive to 6th March 1992. That is the date of their declaration of independence. We have taken the place of the Socialist Republic and, therefore, we are a party to the Convention of Geneva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you again, but this may be a convenient point just to see if I understand where your theory leads. Take World War II, invasion of Denmark, clearly, an international conflict, when Germany invades Denmark, but no hostilities and, indeed, nothing happens for perhaps two years. Germany occupies Denmark. Then acts take place that might well be regarded as grave breaches. Would you say that the time has passed, there is no conflict whatever occurring in Denmark, and had not been for two years, so that the grave breaches provision would not apply? It would cease to be an area to which the Convention applied?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would not say so. If the Germans entered Denmark in your example but did not enter into Jutland, which is an island between Denmark and Sweden, and let us just presume that people of German descent living on Jutland took over, and there was some fight between those people living on Jutland being of German descent and being of Danish descent, I would say it was not a conflict, armed conflict, of an international character. Because the Germans did not come in, they stayed on the mainland, and it was the civilian people who started fighting amongst each other. That is what I am arguing in the Opstina of Prijedor. What happened outside on the mainland of Bosnia did not happen on the island of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not follow the analogy because the JNA had at some stage earlier than 19th May been present in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All over the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All over Bosnia. They did not destroy anything at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When that happened, it was after 19th, and then we have to see where these parts of the JNA in Muslim controlled area, because there was a conflict going on between those parts, not retracting but remaining on the spot, or whatever did they do to help the Bosnian Serbs living in that area, but that did not occur in the area of Prijedor. This was no conflict of this type -- absolutely none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: My question is, and I am not much of a history buff and I always turn to Judge Stevens because he really is, but what I know a little bit is that sometimes in wars, particularly in recent wars, people retake, they lose towns, they go back and forth, you know. It is not like in the old days where you had these ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is dynamic; it is not static.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- whatever, what do you call those, moats, or whatever, where people would get in there. No, it is not fluid now, so it goes and comes. I can see this happening, just going and coming, that is, the Muslims may retake a particular town, then they might lose it and then they might retake it. What you are asking us to do is to take a snap shot and freeze this at a particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There has never been a front line in the neighbourhood of Prijedor and nor has it been in the area of Prijedor. The front line was never there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I do not mean a front line. What I mean is just going back and forth, in just taking control and losing control. You are just saying that is contrary to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It did not happen. It was taken over on April 30th which is also in the report of Gow, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I was arguing that the opinion as I expressed before remains unaltered by the fact that the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a contracting party to the Geneva Convention IV, and it will also be unaltered by the fact that the Muslim government signed on 31st December 1992 retroactive to 6th March being a party to the Geneva Convention, since the status of contracting party does not change an armed conflict in one's own territory to an armed conflict of international character. It is in this issue, it is, of course, not relevant. Now I come to the second question which I raised in relation to Article 2 of the statute, that is, has the grave breaches provision been brought into force by special agreement between the parties? If it was not an armed conflict of an international character, then the parties may bring into force the grave breaches by agreement. So we have to discuss that matter too. Contrary to what the Prosecution seems to be suggesting, the Defence is of the opinion that the agreement of 22nd May 1992 under common Article 3 does not refer to Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV, so that this agreement only provides for a limited protection of civilians in the context of common Article 3. I recall -- I will elaborate it later on -- that Article 2 of the Statute does not include any breach of common Article 3; it only refers to Article 2 of the Geneva Convention. So the agreement of 22nd May, in that agreement there is not any reference to the grave breaches provision. In the opinion of the Defence, the unilateral declarations of 27th August 1992 did not constitute an agreement common Article 3, it not being a declaration of an international legal nature. The documents were signed a titre personnel. The documents not being an agreement under common Article 3, the general reference to the Geneva Convention by itself was, of course, insufficient to bring into force the provision of Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV. In case the unilateral declarations have brought into force the provisions of Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV, quod non, it should be pointed out that this took place after the conduct of which Mr. Tadic is accused, because that period ended on August 3rd and these declarations were made up on a later date in August. So it seems to me that also in that perspective these declarations are irrelevant for the jurisdiction in this specific case. Taking all this into account, it is the submission of the Defence that the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction under Article 2 of the Statute in the case of Dusko Tadic. I will now proceed to Article 3 of the Statute: The Prosecution and the Defence do not differ, I hope, in their opinion concerning the question of what is the basis of Article 3 of the Statute. As far as Article 3 of the Statute relates to the Regulations on land warfare annexed to The Hague Convention regarding the law and customs of war on land of 1907, to the Statute of the International Military Tribunal of Nuremberg and possibly also to some provisions of the 1977 Protocol 1, its application is, as we submitted in our brief, limited to situations of an international armed conflict. There we have different opinions between the Defence and the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, before you get to the next argument, just one question finally on the applicability of grave breaches. You do say that the agreement that was signed was August 27th, I guess it is 1992, is that correct? You say that was after the period. But if the parties did agree to be bound by the grave breaches of the Convention, is that sufficient or need the Chamber then go on to find, assuming we have to find, that it was an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No. What we have argued is that this unilateral declaration is not sufficient to establish a criminal responsibility for an individual under Article 3 in relation to Article 2 of the Geneva Convention. But even if you might find so, we dispute that; we say it is irrelevant because it occurred after the latest charged offence and there was no retroactive provision in it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is a statement to be bound, it is a statement by the parties to be bound, henceforth; is that the way you would read the argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not a recognition that they -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely none whatsoever, no. Dealing with Article 3 of the Statute now and referring to the basis and the difference in opinion related to the question whether the application is limited to situations of an international armed conflict, I may proceed to the next issue: As far as the international conflict, I will confine myself to referring to my expose I made earlier this afternoon on the nature of the conflict and the relevance of place and time, the role of the JNA and the remaining parts and the relevance of all this for Mr. Tadic, you will have to judge this relation with an international armed conflict also in that context when we deal with Article 3 of the Statute. As is apparent from the response, the Prosecution starts from the presumption that Article 3 of the Statute also refers to internal armed conflicts, so I have to deal with that position. This opinion of the Prosecution is founded on statements delivered by the permanent members of the Security Council, that went further than the Secretary-General's commentary explaining the draft Statute in his report of 3rd May 1993. We submit that this is not a correct founding for such an opinion. We submit that the statements of these members do not carry authority and certainly do not bring into force well established international law as required for the establishment of a valid jurisdiction in a criminal case. The report of the Secretary General is quite clear on this point. If I may quote, the relevant part of paragraph 34: "The international tribunal should apply Rules Of international law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law". Whereas the Security Council adopted the draft Statute on the basis of the Secretary-General's report without any alteration, the statements of some members at the time of voting should not be taken into account when the Tribunal seeks guidance in its interpretation of the Statute. But even in the case that the statements bring into force well established international law, we dispute that. We suggest that the principle of legality implies that this "new law" which has only "come into existence", if so, after the actions of which Mr. Tadic is accused took place, cannot refer to the period from 27th May until the 3rd August 1992, because that would be opposite to the principle that you cannot prosecute people on the basis of laws which were accepted at a later date.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But is not common Article 3 a part of customary international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We do not think so. I will come to that point later. We maintain ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The member-states of the Security Council cannot by their own actions just amend, so to speak, the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, they did not. They accepted the Statute as it was and, therefore, we feel that the declaration during the voting process does not well establish international law. They cannot make new law. In the Statute itself, as we have to understand the Statute through the commentary report of the Secretary General, common Article 3 is certainly not a part of Article 3 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But Madeline Albright, Sir Hannay and someone else ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not impressed by which they say. They are ambassadors and they serve the interests of their own countries, but by just making those statements they do not establish international law that works back in time. They express their opinion that it is well-established international law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If Article 3, common Article 3, is a part of customary international law ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And if is it considered under the rubric of laws and customs of war, then I do not understand how you are saying that what they said decided in 1993 something new. Instead was that not simply an expression of what had been existing for a long period of time which would include the period of the alleged offences in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are perfectly right if the Defence accepts that Common Article 3 is well-established international law as a part of ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of customary international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I agree with you I do not know that the permanent representatives can all of a sudden by their declarations create ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is the only argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- customary international law. That perfectly sounds reasonable, but if they are merely stating what the state of the law was, then Common Article 3 goes in to Article 3 of our Statute. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If it was well-established customary international law then I would not have discussed their statements because it would be irrelevant. It was already a part of accepted customary law, but we dispute that Common Article 3 is a part of customary law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In that respect we say it is irrelevant what they have said about it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I presume then from that it is your position that this Tribunal has jurisdiction, if it was validly establish, to try all acts that are a part of customary international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have that jurisdiction? OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: With the provisions you already made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We submit that individual liability cannot simply be brought in afterwards, provided that we dispute this common Article 3, merely by the motivation of votes in which a permanent member gives an interpretation which does not represent customary international law and that would violate, as I already said, the principle nullum crimen sine lege. If I come to the heart of the matter, that is what about common Article 3? We take the position that there is no basis for individual criminal liability for the breach of rules and principles of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, or of the provisions of Protocol 2 which may possibly have become part of international customary law. Neither in these instruments, nor in state practice nor that of any international organisation or any entity, nor any doctrine, can one find a clearly accepted basis for or consensus on the existence of individual criminal responsibility for breach of these rules and principles. We did not find them. I may quote again or refer to Professor Meron in his editorial comments on in the American Journal of International Law of 1994 volume 88, page 83. We think we may say the following. We think that since it has been stressed that reference to the domestic practice of Yugoslavia will be limited to the question of punishment, it is not sufficient to argue that the Tribunal has jurisdiction to apply the minimum standard contained in common Article 3, it being a treaty obligation both of the Former Yugoslavia and of its relevant successor states. We do agree with professor Meron when he made this observation. The laws and customs of law applicable in internal conflicts do not include the system of criminal liability for the breach of these Rules or the prosecution of individuals for a breach of common Article 3 of the Laws and Customs of War as a war crime either. In our opinion, the Prosecution has not demonstrated conclusively that the draft code of crimes against peace and security of mankind and, more especially, Article 22 that these provisions do belong to well-established international law. We suggest that they do not belong to customary international law. In sum, the Defence therefore submits that as far as Article 3 of the Statute is concerned, the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction in the case of Mr. Tadic. That brings me to Article 5 of the Statute. As we have made clear in our brief, the Tribunal only has jurisdiction under Article 5 of the Statute if it involves crimes that have been committed in the execution of or in connection with an international armed conflict. Criminal liability that would go beyond the lines of well-established customary law and would include the crimes that are mentioned here committed during an internal conflict is, as we have stated contrary, to the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. In this respect I would like to remind your Honour of what I said at the beginning of my commentary regarding the status of the Tadic-case. It is a criminal case, so the strict rules of legality and legitimacy apply. In the American Journal of International Law James O'Brien points out that the United Nations has not endorsed the definition of crimes against humanity that severs such crimes from armed conflicts (See his article Current Developments page 649). In his analysis of this issue, James O'Brien does not make any reference to an absolute absence of any requirements of a nexus between crimes against humanity and armed conflict. In his view, the bottom line is that some relation is required in any case. Well, if so, the nexus with an armed conflict implies the requirements of an international armed conflict. In that case I can confine myself again to referring to what I said earlier on the nature of the conflict in Prijedor, namely that conduct of which Mr. Tadic is accused at the time and at places mentioned in the indictment cannot have taken place in relation with or during an international conflict. For this reason we also submit that regarding Article 5 of the Statute, the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction in the case of Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not at all follow what you are saying about Article 5 and its specific reference to whether international or internal. Why does that not answer your submission, or have I misunderstood what you have said about Article 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is hard to understand if someone else misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help you. Mr. Wladimiroff are you saying Article 5 requires that the offences be committed during an armed conflict, because that is what Article 5 says, and the Secretary General's report speaks in terms of that and James O'Brien, I do not know whether he is with State Department or whatever, wherever he is, but he says that too. So there is a requirement of armed conflict you say. Further you say that that conflict must be international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is that step I do not follow at all. It says: "When committed in armed conflict whether international or internal in character."

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And that goes far beyond what is well-established customary international law, and we do not step that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: This is the jurisdiction that has been given to us by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We dispute ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So you are saying, in effect ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- again that the Security Council acted, what, beyond its power because it created retrospective liability? Is that the submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is the submission, but it has also another aspect, that even if you do not feel in the position to review this decision of the Security Council, you have to decide for yourselves whether you will apply law you may have been granted which is contrary to a principle of criminal law, and we suggest that you will not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about that then. You earlier said that we, as the Tribunal, have jurisdiction to apply all customary international laws. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If it raises an individual criminal liability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it calls for criminal liability. So in a sense, the way that the Secretaries General has characterised these laws is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Why is that irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For example, you say that it has been characterised as an armed conflict, whether international or internal in character, and you say he is wrong, that it must be international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because customary international law is that there is an armed conflict required and it must be international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Then I have not made myself very clear. The position that has been taken by the Secretary General was not taken in the context of applicability of the Hague Convention or the applicability of the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am talking about crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, Article 5.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So what you are telling us is it said "whether international or internal", this what Judge Stephen was asking you, but he is wrong that it must be international. I understand your position in that regard and that is why I am asking you how the Chamber is limited to the way that the Secretary General, well, the Security Council since they approved the Statute, defines the offence, so to speak. Must we then find that it is international because you say that it is contrary to customary international law to allow crimes against humanity, adjudication of crimes against humanity in an armed conflict if it is only internal? Must we find it is international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because it is contrary to customary international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not as far as it imposes a criminal liability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So our guide is customary international law; not the way that the Secretary General may have characterised these. OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, the Prosecutor has -- I guess no one likes the way that the Secretary General has characterised it because the Prosecutor says, well, he was wrong to require armed conflict because that is contrary to customary international law. Instead the genocide conventions and torture, apartheid and all of those, they do not require armed conflict and they are a subset of crimes against humanity. So you, Chambers, should just forget about the fact that he put in armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So I guess we then have to decide what in fact is customary international law be guided by that rather than the characterisation of the Secretary General, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the Prosecution is able to show any authority, then your Chamber might accept that it is a part of well-establish international law. I told you we did not find it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So it is presumed not to be well-established international law unless we are informed by literature, opinions, quotations, whatever. None whatsoever I have found.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So if you agree that it is customary international law, then it is OK I guess from your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which is perfectly understandable. Now common Article 3, is that part of customary international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not if it implies individual criminal liability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But if we were to find, contrary to your position, that it is a part of part of customary international law imposing criminal liability, then we would be free to incorporate the acts at least set forth in common Article 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just before you leave this, the Secretary General relies of course on the paramilitary activities in and against Nicaragua. The case of the ICJ bore his conclusion that it does not matter whether it is international or internal in character; that the prohibitions in common Article 3 cannot be breached in an armed conflict. What do you say about that decision or have you not looked at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have not got it in mind at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: His footnote takes one to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I may address that question at a later moment if it pleases you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have made a note of it and I will certainly do that. I think I am almost at the end of my presentation, that is I will bring together Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you bring it together you promised me that you would address the issue of whether or not the position taken by the United States in its amicus curie brief that grave breaches apply even if it is totally internal, not international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is not part of well-established international law. It is part of the argument I already raised. I did not address specifically the amicus curie brief but it is all in the game.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The amicus says in Article 106 -- it says: For example, Article 130 of the 1949 Geneva Convention relative to the treatment of prisoners of war defines ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Excuse me for a minute to find the brief and then I can look for myself. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Page 35, the third full paragraph I think where it begins "Second".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not able to address it at this moment. I think I will do at that also at a later time, maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will have an opportunity after the Prosecutor presents the argument tomorrow afternoon. If you do that and also ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may. Now I am afraid it will not be satisfactory, so I would rather prefer to give it second thought and then give you a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be fine tomorrow, or you can incorporate it as a part of your reply to the Prosecutor. I do not know what they will argue because that is not the position they have taken in their brief; that is the position taken in the amicus. What about the issue of judicialability, the threat to peace? The Security Council has made a determination that the activities in the Former Yugoslavia constituted a threat to peace. I guess my question was, is that the type of issue a judicial Tribunal is in a position to review because it is so fact-based and in a sense it is standardless?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the context of the subject matter it is not a relevant question of course.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We discussed this this morning in the context of the establishment, but in the context of a subject matter problem it seems to me that the real issue is not whether this was a threat to international peace, but was the type of conflict an international one or an internal one. It seems to me that that assessment is a decision you will have to take, and that is not the decision that the Security Council will have to take. Well, as a matter of fact they did not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So their ability to act then under Article 39 is limited to international conflicts; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with each other. What I am trying to say is that the threat to international peace or a threat to peace or a threat to security might be the same as an international or an internal conflict, but it has nothing to do with each other; it is a different concept. Internal conflict might be a risk for security and national peace because it may spread over the border, but not yet. "Not yet" means at that time it is an internal conflict. An international conflict of course is a threat to international peace. There is no doubt about it, but you could not say that it is the same.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are we in a position to review the Security Council's determination that there was a threat to peace?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the context of the first issue of the establishment, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even though they involve factual considerations and another matters perhaps that we are not equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, that is not the bottom of the problem of course, but if prima facie it is clear they could not reasonably think that this was a threat to international security, then the question has been raised this morning whether they have powers under Chapter VII.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I guess my question -- I am not making myself clear. Maybe I am getting an answer and not knowing it -- is whether that is justiceable. You mentioned a number of areas this morning and I did too, activities in Angola, Mozambique, Liberia, all over the world. Sometimes the Security Council has determined that these activities have constituted a threat to peace; sometimes they have chosen not to act, whereas perhaps you and I and any number of other people might, if we were on the Security Council having reviewed the evidence, have found that it was a threat to peace or instead might not have agreed with other members who found it was a threat to peace. Some of these activities have been purely internal, at least conflicts like Somalia purely internal, like Rwanda purely internal. The Security Council has acted in some. In Rwanda they chose to establish a Tribunal looking at a threat to peace that was operating internally seemingly. In Somalia they decided not to establish a Tribunal. Is it appropriate, is that not a non-justiceable political question that courts are not equipped to deal with? This morning I read an opinion by Justice Brennan in a favoured case of mine from the United States and a favoured justice too, Baker v. Carr which talks about these things. That is what really brings it to my mind. Is that something that we as a court should even rule on to determine whether or not they accurately determine that there was a threat to peace?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What we think is that you should not go into the substance of all these issues. It will be impossible by lack of any evidence. What we ask you is to look at the pattern of these problems and what was the consistency of the reactions of the Security Council to such types of problems. In that context, you have to judge on the face of that pattern whether it is reasonable to accept that in this case they understood their own powers as being empowered to establish this Tribunal. If we feel, just to say it very bluntly, that it came just out of the blue, there is no background to understand why they did it, then how come that they understood their own powers, as they did in this case, seeing the history of all the previous decisions? Not going into the details of those resolutions, but trying to understand is it logical as the next step that you establish this Tribunal? If you see the pattern of the positions we dispute that this is a logical next step within the powers. That is what we mean, a martial judgement of what has happened.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is really what you have told us with respect to its selection of the establish of the Tribunal as a measure under 41. It is that same kind of review, is that not so? Mr. Orie may have some good ideas about that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understood what you said this morning. It has to do with establishing a Tribunal to try persons with grey hair. As we look up here we do not want that for sure I suppose!

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am trying to avoid that, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me just to clarify our position on this issue. I think we take the position that the Chamber can review the decision of the Security Council, as we set out this morning, but there might be a difference between the review on the separate questions involved. For example, I can imagine that a review on the powers to establish an ad hoc Tribunal will be far more substantive, and that perhaps the review of the decision as far as justified because of the situation in which it was taken, a direct threat of international peace, I can imagine that the Chamber will be more reluctant. But it is not an argument to say there is no review at all; it is just more a marginal review. For example, if the Security Council would, and I just give a silly example, say tomorrow that because I bought an ice cream in Central Park that was a threat to international peace, I think the Chamber should have the right to review this decision because the basic requirements to be fulfilled in order to take measures under Chapter VII were clearly not present. I think there might be a difference in depth of review of the decision. When we are talking about the establishment of the Tribunal itself, I think it should go far deeper because it is a fundamental question. The question of whether there was a threat to international peace I think is more a question which is influenced by the establishment of facts, by the evaluation of facts. I think that a more marginal approach would be appropriate under these circumstances, but this is not an argument to say that there is no review at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Just some last words to address Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the Statute altogether. As a matter of fact I am summing up now. In sum, the timetable of the offence in 1992 is that on 6th March 1992 Bosnia-Herzegovina declared itself independent. On 7th of April the Bosnian Serbs reconfirmed their declaration of independence, now under the name of Serb Republic. On that same date Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by several states as an independent state. These events triggered the start of the armed conflict. On 27th of April the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was transformed into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On 30th April Prijedor was taken over. On 19th May the JNA was divided into the Yugoslav army withdrawn from Bosnia and amongst others the Serbian army of the Bosnian Serbian Republic. On 22nd May the signature of the London agreement. On 27th August the signature of the unilateral documents. Last, but not least, on 31st December the succession of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a party to the Geneva Convention retroactive 5th March 1992. If we view this timetable and we lay aside the timetable of the charges, we see that the timetable of the charges is, as I already argued, limited to the period of 27th May to 3rd August 1992. That is true because if you look into charge 10, charge 10 occurred, according to the indictment, on 27th May. Charge 4 occurred early June up to the 3rd August. Charge 11 occurred on 14th June. Charge 5 occurred on late June. Charge 8 occurred on late June, early July. Charge 9 occurred on 8th July, charge 10 on 10th July and charge 7 late July. If we understand these timetables, and if we accept the arguments set out before in this presentation, it follows in full conformity to the opinion of the distinguished counsel for the Prosecution, Commander Fenrick, as a member of the Commission of Experts, that the activities, as the Commission of Experts has learned us, occurring in Bosnia-Herzegovina during an armed conflict prior to 6th April "Should be considered", and I quote Mr. Fenrick, "as occurring in an internal conflict." Activities occurring between 6th April and 19th May 1992 "Should be", I quote again Mr. Fenrick, "considered as occurring in an international armed conflict" whilst those, and I quote again Mr. Fenrick, "after 19th May 1992" as occurring during an internal conflict. We have learned that the whole case of Mr. Tadic occurred after May 19th, being in the assessment of the Commission of Experts and in the assessment of a distinguished member of the Prosecution, an internal conflict. You will not be surprised that on the basis of this assessment the Defence takes the position that, whereas all charges allegedly occurred after 19th May 1992, and since common Article 3 does not constitute an individual criminal liability, the Tribunal does not have subject matter jurisdiction in the case of Mr. Tadic. That brings me to the final conclusion and that is the end of our presentation. Our final submission is that the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction in the case of Dusko Tadic, firstly, because as argued this morning it was not established by law; secondly as argued today because it does not have primacy of a domestic court; thirdly as discussed this afternoon because there is no sufficient subject matter jurisdiction. Thank you very much.
